question: How do we measure whether stories can be linked back to real individuals or leak private information, and what methods reduce this re-identification risk?

aspects.name: Story Re-identification Measurement
aspects.description: Papers in this aspect measure whether a generated or transformed story can be linked to a specific real individual. They study attacker models, linkage success, identity inference, and evaluation protocols for narrative text.
aspects.bm25_query: re-identification de-identification anonymization linkage identity inference authorship attribution narrative text privacy attack reidentification
aspects.hyde_abstract: We study how to measure re-identification risk in narrative text that has been anonymized, transformed, or generated from records about real people. We formalize an attacker who links a story to a candidate individual using names, biographical details, writing style, event combinations, and external background knowledge. We introduce evaluation protocols based on top-k identification accuracy, rank-based linkage, membership inference, and calibration across varying candidate-set sizes and attacker knowledge. Experiments on synthetic and real-world personal narratives compare lexical, semantic, stylistic, and hybrid linkage attacks. Results show that removing direct identifiers is insufficient: rare event combinations and narrative style provide strong auxiliary signals, while risk estimates vary substantially with the assumed candidate population. We recommend reporting attacker knowledge, candidate-set construction, and confidence intervals alongside aggregate re-identification scores.

aspects.name: Private Information Leakage
aspects.description: Papers in this aspect detect and quantify whether stories reveal sensitive attributes or confidential facts, even without identifying the person directly. They cover privacy leakage, sensitive-attribute inference, memorization, and inference attacks on narrative content.
aspects.bm25_query: privacy leakage sensitive attribute inference confidential information memorization membership inference disclosure risk personal narratives text privacy-preserving NLP
aspects.hyde_abstract: We investigate privacy leakage from stories that preserve plausible details about real people without explicitly naming them. The study distinguishes direct disclosure, sensitive-attribute inference, membership inference, and reconstruction of confidential events or relationships. We develop an adversarial evaluation framework in which human and automated attackers infer health, legal, financial, demographic, and relational attributes from stories, optionally using retrieved public or auxiliary data. Leakage is measured through attack accuracy, information gain, calibration, and the change in privacy risk relative to a non-sensitive baseline. Across narrative datasets and generation settings, semantic paraphrasing reduces surface memorization but often preserves high-confidence sensitive inferences. The findings demonstrate that privacy evaluation must assess both identity linkage and attribute disclosure, including risks created by combining story content with external knowledge.

aspects.name: Privacy Risk Reduction
aspects.description: Papers in this aspect develop methods that make stories less linkable and less revealing while preserving usefulness, realism, and narrative quality. Relevant techniques include redaction, paraphrasing, differential privacy, synthetic data generation, and controlled text rewriting.
aspects.bm25_query: privacy-preserving text anonymization de-identification redaction pseudonymization differential privacy paraphrasing sanitization synthetic data narrative rewriting
aspects.hyde_abstract: We present a privacy-preserving pipeline for generating and rewriting personal stories while retaining their core narrative utility. The pipeline identifies direct and quasi-identifiers, detects sensitive facts, and applies controlled operations including entity replacement, temporal and geographic generalization, selective redaction, paraphrasing, and synthetic detail generation. We compare rule-based sanitization, neural rewriting, differential privacy, and fully synthetic generation under matched utility constraints. Evaluation combines re-identification and sensitive-attribute attacks with human judgments of coherence, faithfulness, specificity, and perceived usefulness. Results indicate that no single transformation reliably eliminates risk: entity masking protects against simple linkage, whereas generalization and controlled fictionalization are needed against composition attacks. Differentially private generation offers stronger formal guarantees but can reduce fidelity. We show that adaptive, risk-aware editing provides a better privacy–utility trade-off than uniform anonymization.

aspects.name: Privacy Utility Evaluation
aspects.description: Papers in this aspect examine how to compare privacy protections against the quality and usefulness of stories. They establish threat models, privacy–utility trade-offs, human evaluation procedures, and standards for reporting protection and residual risk.
aspects.bm25_query: privacy utility tradeoff narrative quality fidelity coherence usefulness risk assessment threat model anonymization evaluation human study disclosure
aspects.hyde_abstract: We propose a unified framework for evaluating privacy protection in story generation and text anonymization. The framework treats privacy and utility as competing objectives and requires explicit threat models, attacker access assumptions, protected attributes, and downstream uses. Privacy is evaluated with linkage, attribute-inference, membership, and memorization attacks; utility is evaluated through factual consistency, narrative coherence, task performance, diversity, and human judgments of usefulness. We analyze privacy–utility frontiers rather than reporting a single anonymization score, and study how results change with candidate-pool size and auxiliary information. Experiments show that apparent privacy gains can disappear under stronger attackers, while aggressive editing may preserve surface fluency but damage factual and narrative utility. We provide reporting recommendations for reproducible comparisons, including attack budgets, residual disclosure rates, confidence intervals, and stratification by identifier rarity.

question: How is structural similarity in stories captured? How is it defined and what embedding models excel at it?

aspects.name: Structural Similarity Definitions
aspects.description: Papers in this aspect define what makes two stories structurally similar, distinguishing narrative events, plot progression, discourse structure, character roles, and semantic content. They also examine how structural similarity differs from topical or lexical similarity.
aspects.bm25_query: narrative structure structural similarity plot event sequence discourse structure story similarity narrative arcs plot progression character roles semantic similarity
aspects.hyde_abstract: We investigate how structural similarity between stories should be defined independently of shared topics, vocabulary, or surface style. We formalize story structure at multiple levels, including event sequences, causal relations, narrative arcs, discourse relations, character roles, and temporal progression. We compare similarity judgments based on lexical overlap, semantic content, event alignment, and abstract plot organization, using human annotations that separately assess these dimensions. Agreement analyses show that annotators distinguish plot structure from topic similarity, although judgments become less consistent when stories differ in length or narrative perspective. Our results motivate a multidimensional definition of structural similarity in which event ordering, causal dependencies, and role-preserving transformations are central. The analysis provides guidelines for constructing datasets and evaluating embedding models intended to represent story structure rather than only meaning or topic.

aspects.name: Story Structure Representations
aspects.description: Papers in this aspect study how stories are encoded for structural comparison, including event graphs, narrative schemas, situation models, discourse representations, and sequence-based embeddings. The focus is on which structural information is preserved or discarded by each representation.
aspects.bm25_query: story representation narrative representation event graph event chain situation model narrative schema discourse relation plot representation event sequence
aspects.hyde_abstract: We study representations that encode the structure of narrative texts for similarity measurement. We compare sequential event representations with event graphs containing temporal, causal, and coreference links, as well as narrative schemas, situation models, and discourse-based structures. Each representation is converted into a comparable embedding or aligned symbolic form, allowing us to measure which aspects of plot organization are retained. Evaluation uses controlled story pairs that vary event order, causal connectivity, character identity, lexical realization, and narrative style, together with human structural-similarity judgments. Graph-based representations better preserve causal and temporal organization, while sequence representations capture local progression but are sensitive to paraphrase and length. Combining event semantics with relational structure yields the most reliable correspondence between automatic scores and human judgments, demonstrating that structural similarity requires more than pooling sentence or document semantics.

aspects.name: Embedding Models Evaluation
aspects.description: Papers in this aspect evaluate which text embedding models best capture story structure and identify the conditions under which they succeed or fail. They compare sentence, paragraph, document, contextual, contrastive, and instruction-tuned embeddings using structural-similarity metrics and diagnostic tests.
aspects.bm25_query: story embeddings narrative embeddings document embeddings sentence embeddings structural similarity evaluation plot similarity event similarity contrastive learning contextual embeddings
aspects.hyde_abstract: We evaluate whether contemporary text embedding models capture structural similarity in stories rather than merely lexical or topical relatedness. We compare sentence, paragraph, and document encoders, including contextual, contrastively trained, and instruction-tuned embedding models. Models are tested on pairwise story similarity, retrieval, ranking, and controlled perturbation tasks that alter event order, causal relations, character roles, or surface wording while preserving other properties. We report correlations with human judgments, robustness to paraphrase and length variation, and sensitivity to structural violations. Document-level models generally outperform sentence pooling on global plot organization, whereas event-aware and contrastively trained encoders show stronger sensitivity to temporal and causal changes. However, high semantic similarity does not consistently imply structural similarity. The findings establish diagnostic evaluation criteria and show that no single embedding model reliably captures all levels of narrative structure.

question: How do we build personalized agentic systems for education? How do we evaluate them?

aspects.name: Personalized Educational Agents
aspects.description: This aspect covers the design of agentic AI systems that adapt instruction, feedback, content, pacing, and interaction strategies to individual learners. It includes learner modeling, student profiles, pedagogical planning, and multi-turn educational assistance.
aspects.bm25_query: personalized adaptive educational agents tutoring intelligent tutoring systems ITS learner modeling student modeling learner profile knowledge tracing pedagogical planning scaffolding feedback
aspects.hyde_abstract: We study personalized agentic systems for education that adapt instructional decisions to the evolving needs of individual learners. Our system maintains a learner model combining prior knowledge, misconceptions, goals, affective signals, and interaction history, then uses this representation to select explanations, exercises, hints, and feedback through multi-turn interaction. The agent separates pedagogical planning from response generation and updates its strategy after each learner action. We evaluate personalization through learning gains, misconception resolution, task completion, delayed retention, and adaptation quality, comparing the agent with static content and non-personalized tutoring baselines. Results indicate that learner-aware planning improves immediate performance and retention, particularly for students with heterogeneous prior knowledge, while overly aggressive adaptation can reduce learner autonomy. Ablation studies show that explicit learner-state tracking is more important than stylistic personalization.

aspects.name: Agentic Pedagogy and Collaboration
aspects.description: This aspect focuses on how educational agents plan, use tools, manage memory, and coordinate roles such as tutor, coach, evaluator, or peer. It includes single-agent and multi-agent architectures designed around pedagogical theories and learner agency.
aspects.bm25_query: agentic tutoring pedagogical agents educational multi-agent systems tool use planning memory reflection orchestration Socratic dialogue scaffolding metacognition learner autonomy
aspects.hyde_abstract: We investigate agentic architectures for educational interaction, emphasizing pedagogical planning rather than unrestricted answer generation. The proposed system maintains long-term learner memory, decomposes instructional objectives into dialogue actions, invokes retrieval and assessment tools, and selects among tutor, coach, and questioner roles. A controller enforces pedagogical constraints, including eliciting learner reasoning before revealing solutions, adapting scaffolding, and fading support as competence improves. We compare the agent with a direct-answer assistant and a single-role tutor in simulated and human learner studies. Evaluation measures include cognitive engagement, explanation quality, help-seeking behavior, learner autonomy, and learning outcomes. The results show that explicit planning and role specialization improve productive struggle and reduce answer copying, although additional orchestration increases latency and occasionally produces inconsistent conversational goals. The findings highlight the need to align agent policies with established instructional principles.

aspects.name: Educational Agent Evaluation
aspects.description: This aspect covers methods and metrics for evaluating personalized educational agents, including learning effectiveness, interaction quality, personalization, pedagogical appropriateness, safety, and reliability. It includes human studies, longitudinal evaluation, automatic assessment, and learner-centered protocols.
aspects.bm25_query: educational agent evaluation tutoring evaluation learning gains learning outcomes knowledge retention personalization quality human study longitudinal classroom study pedagogical appropriateness
aspects.hyde_abstract: We present a comprehensive evaluation framework for personalized educational agents that distinguishes system quality from educational impact. The framework combines controlled pretest–posttest studies, longitudinal classroom deployment, interaction-level analysis, and expert review. It measures learning gain, delayed retention, transfer, calibration, engagement, agency, satisfaction, fairness, factuality, feedback quality, and the appropriateness of adaptation. We also introduce protocols for evaluating whether an agent’s learner model is accurate and whether its actions improve outcomes for students with different backgrounds and proficiency levels. Across several instructional settings, conventional response-quality metrics correlate weakly with delayed learning and fail to detect harmful over-scaffolding. Human-centered and longitudinal measures provide a more reliable assessment of educational value, while automated rubric-based judgments are useful for scalable monitoring when calibrated against expert annotations. The study argues that educational agents require outcome-based evaluation rather than chatbot-style benchmarks alone.

aspects.name: Safety Equity and Trust
aspects.description: This aspect addresses the risks and governance requirements of personalized educational agents, including privacy, bias, transparency, student well-being, overreliance, accessibility, and equitable performance. It covers safeguards needed for deployment in real educational settings.
aspects.bm25_query: educational AI safety privacy student data algorithmic bias fairness equity trustworthy explainability transparency consent child safety overreliance accessibility
aspects.hyde_abstract: We examine safety, equity, and trust in personalized agentic systems deployed for education. Personalization requires collecting sensitive information about learners, yet inaccurate or biased learner models can produce unequal instruction, inappropriate feedback, and harmful inferences about ability or motivation. We propose a governance framework combining data minimization, consent, access control, uncertainty-aware learner modeling, explanations of adaptive decisions, escalation to human educators, and continuous subgroup auditing. Evaluation includes privacy leakage tests, demographic performance gaps, calibration, harmful-content audits, accessibility checks, and surveys of student and teacher trust. Results show that personalization benefits are uneven when systems are optimized only for average learning gains, with larger errors for less represented learners and multilingual students. Exposing uncertainty and providing educator oversight improves appropriate reliance without eliminating the benefits of adaptation. The findings support treating safety and equity as core educational outcomes rather than post-deployment constraints.

question: How do we build deep research agents? How do we evaluate every component of deep research agents?

aspects.name: Agent Architecture and Workflow
aspects.description: Papers in this aspect study the overall design of deep research agents, including iterative research workflows, planning, decomposition, memory, and coordination between specialized components. They address how agents turn open-ended questions into multi-step investigations and produce grounded reports.
aspects.bm25_query: deep research agent research agent architecture workflow planning task decomposition iterative investigation orchestration memory multi-step
aspects.hyde_abstract: Deep research agents must transform broad information needs into reliable, multi-step investigations rather than answer questions in a single generation pass. We present a modular architecture that decomposes research questions, plans searches, maintains an evidence-aware workspace, revises intermediate hypotheses, and synthesizes a cited report. The agent separates planning, information acquisition, evidence management, and writing while allowing feedback between stages. We evaluate the architecture on diverse open-domain research questions using measures of subquestion coverage, source quality, factuality, citation correctness, and report completeness, together with human judgments of usefulness. Controlled ablations show that iterative replanning and explicit evidence state substantially improve research completeness and reduce unsupported claims, while excessive decomposition increases cost without consistent gains. The findings provide design principles for building scalable, inspectable deep research systems.

aspects.name: Search Browsing and Evidence
aspects.description: This aspect covers the information-acquisition components of deep research agents: query generation, web search, browsing, source selection, evidence extraction, and citation grounding. It examines how agents find diverse, authoritative, and relevant evidence across multiple retrieval steps.
aspects.bm25_query: web search browsing information retrieval query generation source selection evidence extraction citation grounding provenance relevance authority diversity multi-hop retrieval
aspects.hyde_abstract: Research agents depend on search and browsing decisions that determine which evidence enters the reasoning process. We study an agent that generates diverse queries, navigates search results and linked pages, extracts claim-level evidence, and records provenance for every retrieved passage. The system combines multi-hop retrieval with source-quality estimation and adaptive stopping, enabling it to distinguish supporting evidence from merely relevant text. Evaluation uses retrieval recall, source authority, evidence sufficiency, passage-level attribution, citation entailment, and robustness to noisy or conflicting sources. We compare single-shot retrieval, iterative browsing, and browsing with explicit evidence verification. Results indicate that query diversity improves recall, while source-quality filtering and claim-level evidence extraction primarily improve citation precision and factual support. However, longer browsing trajectories can amplify early retrieval errors, motivating verification-aware search policies.

aspects.name: Planning Tools and Synthesis
aspects.description: Papers here investigate the reasoning and execution mechanisms that let agents use tools, manage uncertainty, resolve conflicting evidence, and synthesize long-form research reports. The focus is on reliable coordination between search, analysis, verification, and final writing.
aspects.bm25_query: tool use planning execution function calling uncertainty verification conflict resolution evidence synthesis report generation citation attribution long-form
aspects.hyde_abstract: A deep research agent must coordinate heterogeneous tools and convert fragmented evidence into a coherent, uncertainty-aware report. We propose a controller that selects search, browsing, extraction, calculation, and verification actions using explicit subgoals and confidence estimates. Retrieved claims are stored in an evidence graph linking sources, entailment relations, contradictions, and unresolved questions; a synthesis module then generates a structured report with claim-level citations and calibrated uncertainty. We evaluate tool-selection accuracy, execution success, contradiction detection, numerical reasoning, citation completeness, factual consistency, and human-rated report quality. Experiments across research questions requiring multiple tool types show that evidence-graph mediation reduces citation drift and unsupported synthesis compared with unconstrained tool calling. Verification improves reliability most when triggered selectively, although poorly calibrated confidence can cause premature stopping and incomplete investigations.

aspects.name: Component-Level Evaluation
aspects.description: This aspect develops evaluation frameworks that separately measure every major component of a deep research agent and connect component failures to end-to-end quality. It includes automatic metrics, human protocols, error taxonomies, cost and efficiency measures, and ablation-based diagnosis.
aspects.bm25_query: deep research evaluation component-level evaluation framework agent benchmark planning retrieval browsing reasoning citation factuality completeness faithfulness cost
aspects.hyde_abstract: Existing evaluations often score only the final research report, obscuring whether failures arise from planning, retrieval, browsing, evidence extraction, reasoning, or writing. We introduce a component-level evaluation framework that traces an agent’s trajectory and evaluates subquestion coverage, query quality, retrieval recall, source authority, evidence entailment, claim verification, citation correctness, report completeness, factuality, latency, and token cost. The framework combines automatically checkable annotations with expert judgments and links intermediate errors to final-answer defects. We assess several research-agent configurations through controlled component ablations and error propagation analysis. Results show that end-to-end report quality is most strongly associated with evidence sufficiency and citation entailment, whereas aggregate task scores conceal substantial variation in retrieval and planning behavior. The framework supports reproducible diagnosis, targeted improvement, and cost-reliability comparisons.

aspects.name: End-to-End Research Benchmarks
aspects.description: This aspect studies benchmarks and evaluation protocols for complete deep research agents on realistic, open-ended research tasks. It addresses task difficulty, multi-hop evidence requirements, temporal and source diversity, reproducibility, and holistic assessment of the final research product.
aspects.bm25_query: research agent benchmark open-ended question answering multi-hop research report evaluation factuality completeness citation correctness source quality reproducibility
aspects.hyde_abstract: Deep research agents require evaluation settings that reflect realistic investigations rather than short-answer question answering. We propose a benchmark of open-ended research tasks requiring question interpretation, multi-hop search, heterogeneous sources, evidence comparison, and cited synthesis. Each task includes a rubric for coverage, factual accuracy, source quality, citation entailment, citation completeness, reasoning transparency, and efficiency, while allowing agents to use different tools and workflows. Evaluation combines reference-based checks, claim-level verification, expert ratings, and adversarial tests involving ambiguous questions, conflicting sources, and changing information. Analysis across systems reveals that strong final prose can mask incomplete evidence collection and citation errors, making multidimensional scoring essential. We further report reproducibility and cost variance across runs, showing that research-agent evaluation should measure both answer quality and the stability of the investigative process.

question: Where do hallucinations in LLMs come from? Is it in the training data? How can we combat it?

aspects.name: Data and Training Origins
aspects.description: This aspect covers how pretraining data quality, provenance, coverage, contamination, and distributional gaps contribute to hallucinated LLM outputs. It also examines how training objectives, memorization, and fine-tuning shape factual reliability.
aspects.bm25_query: hallucination factuality pretraining data provenance data quality coverage contamination memorization distribution shift knowledge gaps training objective
aspects.hyde_abstract: Large language models frequently generate fluent claims that are unsupported by their training evidence. We investigate whether hallucinations originate in pretraining data and examine the roles of noisy sources, duplicated or contaminated documents, incomplete coverage, temporal knowledge gaps, and distribution shift. We compare models trained with standard next-token prediction against models exposed to filtered, deduplicated, provenance-aware, and temporally balanced corpora. Using attribution analysis, memorization tests, closed-book factuality evaluations, and source-supported generation assessments, we separate unsupported claims caused by absent knowledge from errors caused by conflicting or misleading evidence. Our findings indicate that data curation reduces several classes of hallucination, but cannot eliminate failures arising from probabilistic decoding and weak grounding. We release diagnostic protocols linking hallucination types to measurable properties of pretraining data.

aspects.name: Generation and Hallucination Mechanisms
aspects.description: This aspect examines why LLMs produce false, fabricated, or unsupported content despite linguistic fluency, including decoding, uncertainty, calibration, knowledge retrieval, reasoning, and instruction-following failures. It also covers taxonomies and reliable evaluation of hallucinations.
aspects.bm25_query: hallucination factuality faithfulness attribution uncertainty calibration decoding generation fabrication unsupported claims factual consistency evaluation
aspects.hyde_abstract: Hallucinations are often treated as a single failure mode, although factual errors, unsupported reasoning, citation errors, and fabricated entities may arise from different mechanisms. We develop a taxonomy of hallucinations and analyze their relationship to model uncertainty, token-level probability, calibration, decoding strategies, chain-of-thought reasoning, and instruction-following behavior. Experiments across open-ended generation, question answering, summarization, and knowledge-intensive prompts measure claim-level factuality, entailment, citation correctness, abstention quality, and human judgments. We find that high likelihood is not a reliable indicator of truth, while semantic uncertainty and disagreement across sampled generations provide stronger signals for some error types. Retrieval reduces errors when evidence is relevant and correctly used, but can introduce citation and interpretation failures. These results motivate mechanism-specific evaluation rather than a single hallucination score.

aspects.name: Hallucination Mitigation
aspects.description: This aspect covers interventions that reduce hallucinations at training time and inference time, including retrieval grounding, supervised and preference tuning, verification, tool use, constrained decoding, uncertainty-aware abstention, and feedback-based correction.
aspects.bm25_query: hallucination mitigation factuality alignment retrieval-augmented generation RAG verification self-correction abstention calibration preference optimization reinforcement learning tool use grounding
aspects.hyde_abstract: We study a unified framework for mitigating hallucinations in large language models through evidence grounding, uncertainty estimation, verification, and selective abstention. The framework retrieves relevant documents, generates claim-level citations, checks entailment with an independent verifier, and declines to answer when evidence is insufficient. We compare retrieval-augmented generation, supervised fine-tuning, preference optimization, self-consistency, tool use, constrained decoding, and post-generation revision across factual question answering and long-form generation. Evaluation jointly measures factual accuracy, evidence entailment, citation precision, helpfulness, coverage, latency, and abstention calibration. Results show that no intervention dominates across settings: retrieval is most effective for externally verifiable knowledge, while verifier-guided abstention improves reliability under missing evidence. Combining grounding with calibrated refusal substantially lowers unsupported claims, but aggressive correction can reduce recall and introduce over-refusal.

question: What are the most effective post-training methods for building domain-specific agents?

aspects.name: Domain Instruction Tuning
aspects.description: Papers in this aspect study supervised post-training for adapting general-purpose models to specialized domains, including domain instruction tuning, continued pretraining, and synthetic or expert-curated demonstrations. They examine how data composition, parameter-efficient tuning, and domain knowledge affect agent performance.
aspects.bm25_query: domain-specific domain adaptation instruction tuning supervised fine-tuning SFT continued pretraining DAPT parameter-efficient PEFT LoRA demonstrations synthetic data
aspects.hyde_abstract: We study supervised post-training strategies for constructing agents specialized to technical and professional domains. We compare domain-adaptive pretraining, supervised fine-tuning on expert demonstrations, synthetic instruction generation, and parameter-efficient updates under matched compute and data budgets. Agents are evaluated on domain question answering, information extraction, grounded decision making, and task completion, with separate tests for factuality, calibration, and robustness to out-of-distribution requests. Results show that targeted supervised fine-tuning substantially improves domain instruction following, while continued pretraining is most beneficial when the domain contains distinctive terminology and document structure. Combining curated expert trajectories with synthetic coverage yields better generalization than scaling synthetic data alone. Parameter-efficient tuning approaches approach full fine-tuning quality while reducing storage and training costs, but remain sensitive to demonstration quality and domain shift.

aspects.name: Preference And Reinforcement Learning
aspects.description: Papers in this aspect investigate post-training agents with human, expert, AI, or environmental feedback, including preference optimization and reinforcement learning. The focus is on aligning domain behavior with expert standards, safety constraints, utility, and long-horizon task outcomes.
aspects.bm25_query: preference optimization RLHF reinforcement learning from human feedback RLAIF DPO direct preference optimization reward modeling expert feedback domain alignment policy optimization
aspects.hyde_abstract: We investigate preference-based and reinforcement-learning methods for adapting agents to specialized domains where correctness depends on expert judgment and operational constraints. We compare reinforcement learning from human feedback, reinforcement learning from AI feedback, direct preference optimization, and outcome-based policy optimization using domain-specific comparisons, scalar rewards, and execution feedback. Evaluation combines expert preference judgments with task success, factual accuracy, constraint satisfaction, and behavioral safety on multi-step workflows. Preference optimization improves response quality with fewer training interactions, whereas reinforcement learning provides larger gains when rewards are obtained from tool execution or delayed task outcomes. Expert-labeled feedback is particularly important for subtle domain conventions and safety decisions. We further find that reward-model errors and preference inconsistency can produce overconfident specialization, motivating calibrated evaluation and mixed-domain validation.

aspects.name: Tool Use And Trajectory Learning
aspects.description: Papers in this aspect study post-training agents to plan, call tools, interact with environments, and complete multi-step domain workflows. They cover trajectory supervision, tool-use fine-tuning, self-improvement, and learning from execution success or failure.
aspects.bm25_query: tool-use agent trajectory learning function calling planning action supervision workflow execution feedback self-improvement environment interaction multi-step
aspects.hyde_abstract: We present a post-training framework for building domain-specific agents that reliably use tools across long-horizon workflows. The framework combines supervised learning from successful interaction trajectories, contrastive training on failed actions, and online updates from execution outcomes. Domain tools are represented through typed schemas and natural-language descriptions, while training emphasizes decomposition, argument validity, recovery, and stopping decisions. We evaluate agents on realistic multi-step tasks requiring retrieval, structured data manipulation, external computation, and interaction with domain software. Compared with response-only instruction tuning, trajectory-based post-training improves tool selection, argument accuracy, recovery from tool errors, and end-to-end completion. Ablations show that diverse failure trajectories and outcome-aware feedback are more valuable than simply increasing the number of successful demonstrations. Gains remain strongest when held-out workflows share tools but differ in task composition.

aspects.name: Effectiveness And Robustness Evaluation
aspects.description: Papers in this aspect develop or apply evaluations that determine whether post-trained domain agents are genuinely effective rather than merely better at static benchmarks. They measure task success, expert quality, reliability, safety, generalization, and efficiency under realistic domain shift.
aspects.bm25_query: domain agent evaluation task success expert evaluation reliability robustness safety calibration generalization distribution shift long-horizon efficiency human assessment
aspects.hyde_abstract: We develop an evaluation framework for comparing post-training methods for domain-specific agents beyond single-turn accuracy. The framework measures end-to-end task success, expert-rated utility, factual grounding, calibration, constraint adherence, tool-use reliability, cost, latency, and recovery from errors. Agents are tested on in-domain tasks, compositional combinations of familiar tools, and shifted workflows containing unfamiliar terminology or incomplete information. We analyze agreement between automatic metrics, execution-based measures, and expert judgments, and report confidence intervals across tasks and domains. The study finds that improvements on domain question answering often fail to predict workflow success, while trajectory completion and constraint satisfaction are more informative for agent deployment. Robustness evaluations expose over-specialization and reward hacking, supporting multi-dimensional reporting of effectiveness rather than ranking methods by a single aggregate score.

question: How are LLMs used to generate political stories or narratives, and how is their capability evaluated?

aspects.name: Political Narrative Generation
aspects.description: Papers in this aspect study how large language models generate political stories, campaign messages, news narratives, speeches, propaganda, and other persuasive political content. They examine prompting, conditioning, personalization, and narrative structure.
aspects.bm25_query: political narrative generation storytelling campaign messaging speeches propaganda news framing persuasive content prompt conditioning personalization large language models LLMs
aspects.hyde_abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to generate political narratives, including campaign messages, speeches, partisan news stories, and persuasive social-media content. We study how prompting and conditioning affect narrative structure, issue framing, emotional appeals, and audience targeting. We construct a controlled corpus of politically themed prompts varying ideology, actor, issue, and intended audience, then compare generated texts across model families and decoding settings. Evaluation combines human judgments of coherence, political relevance, persuasiveness, and rhetorical quality with automated analyses of framing, sentiment, moral appeals, and narrative components. Results show that models produce fluent and internally coherent stories, but their political framing is highly sensitive to prompt wording and audience specifications. Generated narratives also exhibit recurring persuasive templates and uneven ideological coverage, highlighting both the utility and risks of LLM-based political communication.

aspects.name: Political Bias And Persuasion
aspects.description: Papers in this aspect investigate whether generated political narratives express ideological bias, stereotypes, partisan framing, misinformation, or persuasive influence. They also examine how generation changes when models are instructed to target different demographics or political positions.
aspects.bm25_query: political bias ideology partisan framing persuasion misinformation propaganda influence demographic targeting viewpoint neutrality ideological stereotypes polarization generative AI LLM
aspects.hyde_abstract: This paper examines whether large language models generate political narratives that are ideologically biased or disproportionately persuasive. We prompt several systems to produce equivalent stories from opposing partisan viewpoints and to tailor messages to audiences differing in age, political identity, and issue preferences. The analysis measures ideological placement, framing asymmetry, emotional intensity, moral language, factual support, stereotyping, and consistency across repeated generations. Human raters additionally assess perceived neutrality, credibility, persuasiveness, and willingness to share. We find that models can reliably shift narrative framing when explicitly instructed, while residual ideological tendencies remain under neutral prompts. Audience personalization increases rhetorical effectiveness but can also amplify polarization and unsupported claims. These findings motivate evaluations that distinguish controllable viewpoint expression from systematic bias and harmful political persuasion.

aspects.name: Evaluating Narrative Capability
aspects.description: Papers in this aspect develop and compare methods for evaluating LLM-generated political stories, including factuality, coherence, political framing, persuasion, diversity, controllability, and human alignment. They assess the reliability of automatic metrics, human annotation, and model-based judges.
aspects.bm25_query: evaluation political text generation narrative quality factuality coherence faithfulness controllability diversity persuasion human evaluation annotation LLM-as-a-judge automatic metrics
aspects.hyde_abstract: Evaluating political narrative generation requires measuring more than grammatical fluency. We propose a multidimensional framework covering narrative coherence, factuality, source faithfulness, political framing, ideological consistency, persuasiveness, diversity, and controllability. Generated stories are evaluated using expert and crowd annotations, claim-level verification against evidence, classifier-based framing analysis, and comparisons with lexical and embedding-based metrics. We further test whether model-based judges agree with human assessments and whether evaluation changes across prompts, topics, and intended audiences. Experiments show that automatic similarity and fluency scores correlate weakly with political quality and can reward repetitive or misleading narratives. Structured human protocols and claim-level factuality checks provide more reliable estimates, while controllability should be reported separately from overall quality. The framework supports reproducible comparison of systems used for political storytelling and communication.

question: How can knowledge graphs be combined with LLMs to answer complex multi-hop questions?

aspects.name: KG-Enhanced Retrieval
aspects.description: Papers in this aspect use knowledge graphs to retrieve, organize, and ground evidence for large language models before or during question answering. They address entity linking, graph traversal, subgraph retrieval, and hybrid symbolic-neural retrieval for multi-hop queries.
aspects.bm25_query: knowledge graph KG LLM retrieval-augmented generation RAG entity linking subgraph retrieval graph traversal hybrid retrieval grounding
aspects.hyde_abstract: We study how knowledge graphs can improve evidence retrieval for large language models answering complex multi-hop questions. Our approach links question entities to graph nodes, decomposes questions into intermediate relations, and retrieves a minimal connected subgraph using a hybrid combination of dense retrieval, lexical matching, and constrained graph traversal. The retrieved facts are serialized as structured context and supplied to the language model with provenance information. We evaluate retrieval recall, answer accuracy, hop-level support, and citation faithfulness across multi-hop question answering datasets spanning textual and tabular evidence. Results show that graph-guided retrieval recovers relevant intermediate entities more reliably than vector search alone and reduces unsupported answers, particularly when questions require rare entities or long reasoning chains. Ablations demonstrate that entity linking and path constraints are both essential.

aspects.name: Graph-Guided Reasoning
aspects.description: Papers in this aspect investigate how LLMs perform explicit multi-step inference over knowledge graphs rather than merely receiving retrieved facts. They cover query decomposition, path planning, symbolic execution, neuro-symbolic reasoning, and iterative graph interaction.
aspects.bm25_query: multi-hop question answering knowledge graph reasoning path planning query decomposition neuro-symbolic symbolic execution graph traversal LLM chain-of-thought
aspects.hyde_abstract: We present a graph-guided reasoning framework for large language models that decomposes complex questions into executable subqueries over a knowledge graph. The model predicts entities, relations, and intermediate goals, while a symbolic executor validates each step and returns graph neighborhoods for subsequent reasoning. This design separates uncertain language interpretation from exact relational inference and supports variable-length reasoning paths. We evaluate end-to-end answer accuracy, executable path validity, intermediate-step accuracy, and robustness to distractor edges on multi-hop knowledge graph question answering benchmarks. Compared with unconstrained chain-of-thought prompting and retrieval-only baselines, the proposed framework produces more valid paths and improves compositional accuracy, especially for three- and four-hop questions. Error analysis shows that relation ambiguity and early entity disambiguation remain the main sources of failure.

aspects.name: KG-LLM Integration
aspects.description: Papers in this aspect study architectural and training strategies for integrating knowledge graphs into LLMs. They include graph-to-text prompting, graph encoders, adapters, retrieval augmentation, continued pretraining, and joint symbolic-neural representations.
aspects.bm25_query: knowledge graph LLM integration graph neural network GNN graph encoder graph-to-text prompting adapter pretraining retrieval augmentation neuro-symbolic
aspects.hyde_abstract: We investigate strategies for integrating knowledge graph structure into large language models for multi-hop question answering. We compare graph-to-text serialization, graph neural network encoders coupled through lightweight adapters, and retrieval-augmented prompting with explicit triples and paths. Each strategy is trained or prompted to preserve entity identity, relation direction, and neighborhood structure while retaining the language model’s broad linguistic knowledge. Evaluation measures answer accuracy, calibration, robustness to paraphrased relations, and generalization to unseen graph paths. Across settings, structured retrieval provides the strongest low-resource performance, whereas graph encoders offer better robustness when relevant evidence is distributed across several neighborhoods. Combining an adapter with path-aware retrieval yields the best overall trade-off, suggesting that effective systems need both faithful graph access and mechanisms for translating symbolic structure into language-model-compatible representations.

aspects.name: Faithful Answer Verification
aspects.description: Papers in this aspect focus on verifying that LLM answers to multi-hop questions are supported by valid knowledge-graph paths. They address provenance, consistency checking, hallucination detection, answer calibration, and correction of invalid reasoning chains.
aspects.bm25_query: knowledge graph LLM hallucination faithfulness provenance explanation answer verification fact checking consistency calibration evidence path validation
aspects.hyde_abstract: We address the problem of unfaithful answers produced by large language models when reasoning over knowledge graphs. Our system generates candidate answers and reasoning paths, then applies graph-based verification to check entity consistency, relation direction, hop completeness, and support for the final claim. When verification fails, the model revises the answer by retrieving alternative paths or abstaining when evidence is insufficient. We evaluate exact-match accuracy together with factuality, citation precision, path validity, calibration, and selective prediction under incomplete and noisy graphs. Verification substantially reduces unsupported answers and improves the reliability of explanations, although strict path validation can lower recall when the graph omits implicit relations. The results indicate that provenance-aware decoding and calibrated abstention are important complements to graph retrieval and language-model reasoning.

question: What recent techniques improve knowledge distillation from large to small language models?

aspects.name: Distillation Objectives
aspects.description: Papers in this aspect develop improved training signals for transferring capabilities from large teacher language models to smaller students. They cover logits, soft targets, intermediate representations, and alternatives to conventional response imitation.
aspects.bm25_query: knowledge distillation KD teacher student logits soft targets response distillation representation distillation hidden states feature distillation language models
aspects.hyde_abstract: We study how the choice of distillation objective affects the transfer of capabilities from a large language model to a compact student. We compare conventional soft-label distillation with response-level supervision, token-level logits, hidden-state matching, attention transfer, and hybrid objectives that combine these signals. To separate objective quality from data and optimization effects, all students are trained on identical teacher-generated and human-curated corpora under matched compute budgets. Evaluation covers perplexity, instruction following, factuality, reasoning, calibration, and generation quality across multiple held-out tasks. Our results show that token-level distribution matching is most effective for language modeling, while combining output distributions with selective intermediate-state alignment improves generalization on reasoning and transfer tasks. We further find that adaptive weighting is preferable to fixed mixtures, particularly when teacher and student architectures differ substantially.

aspects.name: Data And Transfer Signals
aspects.description: This aspect covers techniques that improve which examples and teacher outputs are used for distillation. It includes synthetic data generation, curriculum learning, data selection, augmentation, and difficult-example or capability-focused sampling.
aspects.bm25_query: knowledge distillation data selection synthetic data teacher-generated curriculum learning hard examples data augmentation self-instruct capability transfer sample selection
aspects.hyde_abstract: We investigate data-centric techniques for improving distillation from large language models into smaller students. Rather than treating the distillation corpus as fixed, we construct training sets through teacher-guided synthesis, uncertainty-aware filtering, diversity selection, curriculum ordering, and targeted generation for underrepresented capabilities. We evaluate these strategies under equal example counts and teacher-query budgets, using both instruction-tuning and domain-transfer settings. Students are assessed on held-out instruction following, knowledge recall, mathematical and multi-step reasoning, robustness, and contamination-sensitive evaluations. The findings indicate that carefully selected synthetic examples consistently outperform indiscriminate teacher generations, with the largest gains arising from examples that expose student weaknesses while preserving diverse linguistic forms. Curriculum schedules provide additional improvements when tasks vary substantially in difficulty, whereas simply increasing the volume of generated data yields diminishing returns.

aspects.name: Efficient Distillation Training
aspects.description: Papers in this aspect propose optimization and systems techniques that make teacher-to-student distillation cheaper, faster, or more effective under limited compute and teacher-inference budgets. They include online and offline distillation, parameter-efficient training, quantization-aware procedures, and compression-aware objectives.
aspects.bm25_query: efficient knowledge distillation online offline distillation teacher inference cost parameter-efficient fine-tuning PEFT quantization-aware distillation low-resource compression
aspects.hyde_abstract: We present a compute-efficient framework for distilling large language models into smaller deployable models under constrained teacher-inference and training budgets. The framework combines offline caching of teacher signals, selective token-level supervision, parameter-efficient student adaptation, and quantization-aware optimization. We compare it with full-corpus online distillation, standard supervised fine-tuning, and post-training compression pipelines while controlling student size, wall-clock training cost, and memory usage. Experiments across general instruction following and domain adaptation show that selective teacher queries preserve most of the quality gains of dense distillation while substantially reducing inference cost. Jointly optimizing distillation and quantization is more reliable than quantizing after training, especially for small students. Ablations further demonstrate that budget allocation should prioritize examples with high teacher uncertainty and large teacher–student disagreement.

aspects.name: Reasoning And Capability Transfer
aspects.description: This aspect focuses on techniques for transferring reasoning, tool-use, factuality, and other emergent capabilities that are difficult to reproduce through ordinary next-token imitation. It includes rationale distillation, process supervision, preference signals, and self-improvement.
aspects.bm25_query: reasoning distillation rationale distillation chain-of-thought process supervision preference distillation tool use self-improvement capability transfer large language models
aspects.hyde_abstract: We examine how distillation can transfer capabilities that are poorly captured by matching final answers alone, with emphasis on multi-step reasoning and tool-assisted problem solving. The student receives combinations of final responses, rationales, intermediate actions, verifier feedback, preference comparisons, and process-level correctness labels produced by a stronger teacher. We compare outcome distillation against process-aware and selectively revealed rationale objectives across arithmetic, symbolic, factual, and tool-use settings. Evaluation measures both answer accuracy and the validity, faithfulness, and efficiency of generated reasoning traces. Process supervision improves difficult reasoning when intermediate annotations are reliable, but unrestricted rationale imitation can propagate teacher errors and increase verbosity. A verifier-guided objective that distills corrected steps and tool decisions achieves the strongest overall transfer, particularly when the student has substantially fewer parameters than the teacher.

question: How reliable are LLMs as automatic evaluators of generated text

aspects.name: LLM Judge Reliability
aspects.description: Papers in this aspect assess whether large language models can consistently and accurately evaluate generated text, often comparing them with human judgments or expert annotations. They examine agreement, validity, calibration, and generalization across generation tasks.
aspects.bm25_query: LLM-as-a-judge evaluator evaluation reliability validity consistency human agreement inter-rater agreement correlation automatic assessment
aspects.hyde_abstract: Large language models are increasingly used as evaluators of generated text, yet their reliability relative to human assessment remains unclear. We study LLM-based judging across summarization, dialogue, translation, and open-ended generation, measuring agreement with expert ratings, rank correlation, pairwise preference accuracy, and test–retest consistency. We compare several judge prompting strategies and evaluate both scalar scoring and pairwise comparison protocols. Our analysis shows that LLM judges can track broad quality differences but exhibit substantially lower reliability on nuanced, subjective, and stylistically diverse examples. Reliability varies with the judge model, evaluation format, and reference availability. Human agreement is strongest for factuality and task completion, while judgments of coherence and helpfulness are less stable. These findings establish practical criteria for interpreting LLM-based automatic evaluation and identify settings in which human oversight remains necessary.

aspects.name: Biases And Instability
aspects.description: Papers in this aspect investigate systematic errors and sources of unreliable LLM evaluation, including position, verbosity, style, self-preference, and prompt sensitivity biases. They also study robustness to adversarial or distribution-shifted generations.
aspects.bm25_query: LLM judge bias position bias verbosity bias length bias self-preference sycophancy prompt sensitivity robustness evaluator reliability
aspects.hyde_abstract: Automatic evaluation with LLM judges may reflect properties of the evaluator rather than the quality of generated text. We characterize position bias, verbosity bias, style preference, self-preference, sycophancy, and sensitivity to prompt wording in model-based evaluation. Using controlled pairs of responses with matched semantic content and independently manipulated length, formatting, fluency, and order, we quantify changes in scores and pairwise preferences. We further test judge behavior under domain shift, low-quality distractors, and adversarially optimized outputs. The results reveal substantial inconsistencies across evaluation protocols: response order and superficial writing style can alter rankings, while longer answers are often favored despite factual errors. Structured prompts and order randomization reduce, but do not eliminate, these effects. We release diagnostic templates for auditing judge reliability.

aspects.name: Evaluation Protocols
aspects.description: Papers in this aspect compare prompting, scoring, and aggregation procedures for using LLMs as evaluators. They focus on rubric design, pairwise versus pointwise judgments, chain-of-thought or structured rationales, reference-based evaluation, and judge calibration.
aspects.bm25_query: LLM evaluation protocol rubric prompt pairwise pointwise scoring reference-based reference-free structured rationale chain-of-thought calibration
aspects.hyde_abstract: The reliability of an LLM evaluator depends not only on the judge model but also on the evaluation protocol. We conduct a systematic comparison of rubric-based prompting, pointwise scoring, pairwise preference judgments, reference-based evaluation, and reference-free assessment. Each protocol is tested with and without explicit criteria, decomposed subquestions, output constraints, and judge calibration against a small set of human-labeled examples. We evaluate agreement with human annotations, ranking accuracy, score variance across repeated runs, and sensitivity to prompt and response order. Pairwise judgments generally provide more stable rankings than unconstrained scalar scores, while decomposed rubrics improve diagnostic validity at the cost of additional inference. Calibration reduces systematic scale differences but does not fully correct content-dependent bias. The study offers recommendations for designing reproducible LLM-as-a-judge pipelines.

aspects.name: Text Quality Dimensions
aspects.description: Papers in this aspect examine how reliably LLM evaluators measure specific qualities of generated text, such as factuality, faithfulness, relevance, coherence, safety, helpfulness, and linguistic quality. They identify which dimensions are easier or harder for automatic judges to assess.
aspects.bm25_query: LLM judge factuality faithfulness hallucination relevance coherence fluency helpfulness harmlessness quality evaluation generated text
aspects.hyde_abstract: LLM judges are often treated as general-purpose evaluators, although different dimensions of generated-text quality may require distinct evidence and reasoning. We measure judge reliability separately for factuality, faithfulness, relevance, coherence, fluency, helpfulness, and safety. For each dimension, we construct evaluation prompts with explicit rubrics and compare model judgments against expert annotations and pairwise human preferences. We analyze correlations, calibration error, false-positive and false-negative rates, and performance under factual conflicts, incomplete references, and stylistic variation. Judges are most dependable when evaluating explicit task compliance and locally verifiable factual claims, but they struggle with subtle omissions, source faithfulness, long-range coherence, and culturally dependent notions of helpfulness. Dimension-specific prompts improve agreement, yet no single judge provides uniformly reliable measurements across all quality criteria.

question: When should LLM systems rely on long-context models versus retrieval-augmented generation or explicit memory mechanisms?

aspects.name: Long-Context Processing
aspects.description: Papers in this aspect study how LLMs use very long input windows, including attention behavior, context utilization, lost-in-the-middle effects, and the accuracy and cost trade-offs of retaining information directly in the prompt.
aspects.bm25_query: long-context extended context context window attention quadratic lost-in-the-middle needle-in-a-haystack context utilization positional encoding extrapolation inference cost
aspects.hyde_abstract: Long-context LLMs offer a direct alternative to external retrieval and memory, but their large nominal context windows do not guarantee reliable use of all supplied information. We study how answer accuracy, faithfulness, latency, and inference cost change as relevant evidence is placed at different positions and mixed with increasing amounts of distractor text. We compare long-context prompting across several transformer-based systems and document lengths, analyzing attention allocation, positional effects, and lost-in-the-middle behavior. We further evaluate whether compression, chunk ordering, and query-focused context selection improve effective context utilization. Results show that direct long-context processing is strongest when evidence is moderately sized, semantically coherent, and available in one pass, but performance degrades with distractors and long-range interference. These findings characterize when a large context window is preferable to external evidence access.

aspects.name: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
aspects.description: Papers in this aspect examine when systems should retrieve external passages or documents instead of placing all available information in the context, including retrieval quality, grounding, freshness, and retrieval-induced generation errors.
aspects.bm25_query: RAG retrieval-augmented generation dense retrieval sparse retrieval hybrid search reranking grounding citation factuality evidence latency index freshness open-domain question answering
aspects.hyde_abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation provides LLMs with selective access to large or changing knowledge collections, potentially avoiding the cost and interference of full-context prompting. We investigate the conditions under which retrieval improves over direct long-context input. Our evaluation varies corpus size, evidence density, document redundancy, knowledge freshness, query ambiguity, and the number of retrieved passages. We measure answer accuracy, attribution, retrieval recall, faithfulness, latency, and token cost, while separately identifying retrieval and generation failures. Retrieval is most advantageous when the knowledge source is large, sparse, frequently updated, or requires provenance, but it can underperform long-context processing when relevant evidence is distributed across many documents or retrieval misses compositional dependencies. Hybrid strategies combining broad retrieval with context compression substantially reduce token usage while preserving grounded answer quality.

aspects.name: Explicit Memory Mechanisms
aspects.description: Papers in this aspect study persistent or structured memory outside the immediate prompt, such as episodic memory, semantic memory, conversation memory, summaries, profiles, and learned memory stores for repeated interactions.
aspects.bm25_query: LLM memory long-term memory persistent memory episodic memory semantic memory conversational memory external memory memory retrieval summarization personalization continual learning
aspects.hyde_abstract: Explicit memory mechanisms allow LLM systems to retain information across interactions rather than repeatedly processing complete conversation histories or relying on parametric knowledge. We compare episodic stores, semantic summaries, structured user profiles, and learned memory modules under multi-session workloads. The study evaluates recall of prior facts, temporal consistency, personalization, contradiction handling, privacy-sensitive deletion, storage growth, update cost, and response latency. We contrast memory access with long-context prompting and retrieval from the full interaction archive, using tasks that require both recent dialogue and durable user-specific information. Structured memory improves repeated-use efficiency and personalization, especially when information recurs across sessions, but introduces write errors, stale beliefs, and governance challenges. The results suggest that explicit memory is preferable for stable, reusable interaction history, while volatile or globally relevant knowledge should remain in retrievable external sources.

aspects.name: System Selection Criteria
aspects.description: Papers in this aspect develop empirical or adaptive policies for choosing among long-context input, retrieval, and explicit memory, considering workload characteristics, quality requirements, latency, token cost, privacy, and information dynamics.
aspects.bm25_query: adaptive routing strategy selection long-context retrieval memory cost latency accuracy quality-aware orchestration query classification uncertainty budget dynamic context allocation agentic systems
aspects.hyde_abstract: LLM applications often support long-context prompting, retrieval-augmented generation, and explicit memory, but the best mechanism depends on the information workload and operational constraints. We propose a routing framework that estimates evidence size, dispersion, freshness, recurrence, privacy, and uncertainty before selecting or combining context access strategies. The router is evaluated on single-document reasoning, multi-document synthesis, evolving knowledge, multi-session personalization, and cost-constrained question answering. We compare fixed long-context, retrieval-only, memory-only, and oracle policies using answer quality, factuality, citation completeness, latency, token consumption, and failure recovery. Adaptive routing approaches the oracle while reducing average context and retrieval costs. Analysis shows that long-context processing is favored by compact, highly interdependent evidence; retrieval by large, sparse, or changing corpora; and explicit memory by durable cross-session facts. The study offers practical decision boundaries for deploying hybrid LLM systems.

question: How is structural similarity in stories captured? How is it defined and what embedding models excel at it?

aspects.name: Defining story structural similarity
aspects.description: Papers that define and operationalize structural similarity between stories, focusing on shared event sequences, plot progression, narrative arcs, character roles, causal relations, and other structural representations rather than shared wording or topics.
aspects.bm25_query: story structural similarity narrative structure plot event sequence narrative arc event relations character roles causal structure plot alignment story similarity
aspects.hyde_abstract: Stories can be similar even when they differ in vocabulary, setting, characters, and surface events. We study how structural similarity in narratives should be defined and operationalized through recurring event sequences, causal relations, character roles, and plot progression. We compare representations based on event graphs, aligned narrative beats, character interaction structures, and abstract plot arcs, distinguishing structural resemblance from lexical overlap, topical similarity, and shared genre. Human judgments on pairs of stories show that annotators rely most strongly on ordered events and causal dependencies, while character identity and local wording are less important. We propose a multi-level annotation scheme and find that structural similarity is best modeled by combining event ordering with relational and narrative-arc information. The analysis provides criteria for evaluating story embeddings that capture plot structure rather than surface content.

aspects.name: Embedding models for story similarity
aspects.description: Papers that develop or evaluate embedding models for capturing structural similarity in stories, including sentence, passage, document, event-based, graph-based, and long-context narrative representations.
aspects.bm25_query: story embeddings narrative embeddings structural similarity plot similarity event embeddings document representations long-context transformers narrative graphs plot alignment
aspects.hyde_abstract: Embedding models for stories often retrieve texts with similar words or topics while missing deeper similarities in plot structure. We evaluate narrative representations for structural story similarity, comparing pooled transformer embeddings, hierarchical long-context encoders, event-centric embeddings, and graph-based representations of characters and events. The evaluation uses human similarity judgments and retrieval settings in which stories share plot patterns but differ in entities, genre, and wording. Models that encode ordered events and causal links outperform standard document embeddings on structural similarity, although hierarchical contextual representations remain competitive for long narratives. Contrastive training with hard negatives that preserve topics but alter event structure produces the largest gains. We further show that performance depends on narrative length and the granularity of event extraction, highlighting the need for evaluations that separate structural, semantic, and lexical similarity.

question: How do we build personalized agentic systems for education? How do we evaluate them?

aspects.name: Building personalized educational agents
aspects.description: Papers on designing and developing agentic systems for education that personalize instruction, feedback, planning, tutoring, or learning activities to individual students. This includes learner modeling, adaptive interaction, memory, tool use, and multi-agent coordination in educational settings.
aspects.bm25_query: personalized agentic systems education educational agents intelligent tutoring learner modeling adaptive tutoring student modeling personalization memory tool use multi-agent
aspects.hyde_abstract: Educational agents must adapt to learners’ knowledge, goals, preferences, pace and affect while maintaining coherent interactions over extended learning activities. We present a personalized agentic tutoring system that combines a learner model, long-term interaction memory, retrieval over instructional resources and planning tools for generating adaptive explanations, exercises and feedback. The agent updates its estimate of student mastery from dialogue, answers and learning behaviors, and selects actions according to both pedagogical objectives and learner preferences. We evaluate the system with students across varied prior knowledge and compare it with non-personalized tutoring and static conversational assistance. Personalization improves learning gains, engagement and task completion, particularly for students with heterogeneous misconceptions, but errors in learner-state estimation can lead to inappropriate scaffolding. Ablation studies show that explicit pedagogical planning and calibrated memory are important for reliable adaptation.

aspects.name: Evaluating personalized educational agents
aspects.description: Papers that evaluate personalized agentic systems for education, including learning outcomes, personalization quality, pedagogical effectiveness, interaction quality, fairness, safety, and longer-term student engagement.
aspects.bm25_query: evaluation personalized agentic systems education educational agents intelligent tutoring learning gains personalization quality pedagogical effectiveness student engagement fairness safety
aspects.hyde_abstract: Evaluating personalized educational agents requires measuring more than conversational fluency or immediate task success. We propose a framework that jointly assesses learning gains, retention, personalization quality, pedagogical appropriateness, interaction experience, equity and safety. The framework combines pretest-posttest learning measures, delayed assessments, expert ratings of instructional decisions, student judgments of adaptation, interaction logs and analyses of differential performance across learner groups. In a controlled study, personalized agents produce larger short-term gains than generic agents, but improvements in perceived helpfulness do not always predict retention. We further find that agents can over-personalize by lowering challenge for struggling students and can perform unevenly across language backgrounds. We recommend reporting learner-level outcomes, longitudinal measures and subgroup analyses alongside standard automatic and human evaluations.

question: How do we build deep research agents? How do we evaluate every component of deep research agents?

aspects.name: Building deep research agents
aspects.description: Papers on designing deep research agents that autonomously decompose questions, retrieve and browse sources, synthesize evidence, and produce grounded research reports. This includes agent architectures, tool use, planning, memory, source citation, and iterative research workflows.
aspects.bm25_query: deep research agents autonomous research agentic search web browsing question decomposition planning retrieval synthesis citations tool use evidence grounding
aspects.hyde_abstract: Deep research agents must go beyond single-step retrieval by decomposing complex questions, searching heterogeneous sources, verifying evidence, and synthesizing findings into coherent reports. We present a modular agent architecture that combines query planning, iterative web search, document reading, evidence tracking, and citation-aware generation. The agent maintains a structured research graph linking claims to supporting passages and revises its search strategy when evidence is incomplete or contradictory. We compare fixed pipelines with adaptive tool-using agents across multi-hop, temporal and synthesis-oriented research questions. Adaptive planning improves source coverage and citation completeness, particularly for questions requiring several dependent searches, while uncontrolled browsing increases cost and exposes the system to irrelevant or low-quality sources. Ablation studies show that explicit evidence tracking and claim-level verification are central to reliable deep research.

aspects.name: Evaluating deep research agents
aspects.description: Papers that evaluate deep research agents at both the overall report level and the component level, measuring planning, retrieval, browsing, reading, evidence attribution, synthesis, factuality, and efficiency. The focus is on diagnostic evaluations that identify which component causes an agent’s successes or failures.
aspects.bm25_query: deep research agent evaluation component-wise planning retrieval browsing evidence attribution citation factuality completeness efficiency benchmark
aspects.hyde_abstract: Evaluating deep research agents requires more than judging the quality of their final reports. We introduce a component-level evaluation framework that separately measures question decomposition, search quality, document selection, evidence extraction, claim verification, citation correctness, synthesis, and computational cost. The framework combines process traces with reference-supported annotations and evaluates both intermediate decisions and final answers on complex research questions. We find that report-level factuality can conceal substantial retrieval and attribution failures: agents may produce plausible summaries while relying on incomplete or weakly relevant evidence. Retrieval recall and citation entailment are the strongest predictors of answer reliability, whereas longer reports are not consistently better. Component ablations and error analyses show that diagnostic evaluation provides more actionable insights than aggregate answer scores for improving deep research agents.

question: Where do hallucinations in LLMs come from? Is it in the training data? How can we combat it?

aspects.name: Origins of LLM hallucinations
aspects.description: Papers that investigate where hallucinations in large language models (LLMs) originate, including decoding uncertainty, knowledge gaps, parametric memorization, distribution shift, and failures of factual grounding. This aspect covers causal analyses of hallucination formation rather than mitigation techniques.
aspects.bm25_query: LLM large language model hallucination factuality causes origins knowledge gaps uncertainty memorization distribution shift grounding calibration decoding
aspects.hyde_abstract: Hallucinations—confidently generated statements that are unsupported or false—remain a central limitation of large language models. We study their origins by separating failures caused by missing parametric knowledge, distribution shift, decoding uncertainty and weak grounding from failures introduced during generation. Across question answering, summarization and open-ended generation, we compare internal confidence, token entropy, retrieval evidence and memorization estimates. Hallucinations are most common when prompts require compositional inference beyond memorized facts, when the input distribution differs from pretraining data, and when decoding favors fluent but weakly supported continuations. High confidence is not a reliable indicator of correctness, particularly for long-form responses. Our analysis suggests that hallucination is a heterogeneous phenomenon arising from interactions between data coverage, model representations and generation dynamics rather than from a single defect.

aspects.name: Training data and hallucinations
aspects.description: Papers that examine how pretraining data quality, coverage, duplication, temporal staleness, contradictions, synthetic text, and source reliability contribute to hallucinations in LLMs. The focus is specifically on links between training-data properties and factual errors.
