aspects.bm25_query: LLM large language model hallucination pretraining data training corpus data quality factual errors contamination duplication contradictions misinformation synthetic data
aspects.hyde_abstract: The relationship between pretraining data and hallucination in large language models is poorly understood. We examine whether factual errors arise from insufficient data coverage, unreliable sources, contradictory documents, duplication, temporal staleness or synthetic text in the training corpus. Using controlled corpus interventions and data attribution, we measure how changes in source composition affect factual question answering and long-form generation. Improving source reliability reduces repeated misinformation, whereas simply increasing corpus size does not consistently improve factuality. Duplicated and conflicting passages can produce unstable answers, especially for entities with changing attributes. We also find that models may hallucinate when relevant facts are present but sparsely represented or surrounded by distracting evidence. These results indicate that data curation and provenance tracking are important, but cannot alone eliminate hallucinations caused by inference and decoding.

aspects.name: Mitigating LLM hallucinations
aspects.description: Papers that develop and evaluate methods for reducing hallucinations in LLMs, including retrieval augmentation, grounding, verification, uncertainty estimation, calibration, constrained decoding, preference optimization, and factuality-oriented training. Methods should target factual reliability in generated outputs.
aspects.bm25_query: LLM large language model hallucination mitigation factuality retrieval-augmented generation RAG grounding verification calibration uncertainty factuality training citation
aspects.hyde_abstract: We investigate a unified framework for mitigating hallucinations in large language models through evidence retrieval, uncertainty estimation and answer verification. The system first retrieves passages from trusted sources, generates a response with explicit citations, and invokes a verifier that can abstain when evidence is insufficient. We compare retrieval-augmented generation, supervised factuality training, preference optimization, calibrated confidence scores and constrained decoding across knowledge-intensive question answering and summarization. Retrieval improves factual accuracy when the corpus contains relevant evidence, while verification and abstention are essential for preventing unsupported claims when retrieval fails. Training-based methods improve in-domain reliability but can reduce coverage on novel questions. We recommend evaluating both factual correctness and appropriate refusal, since systems that answer fewer questions may appear more reliable without providing better evidence-grounded responses.

question: What are the most effective post-training methods for building domain-specific agents?

aspects.name: Post-training methods for domain-specific agents
aspects.description: Papers that develop or compare post-training techniques for building agents specialized to a particular domain, including supervised fine-tuning, instruction tuning, preference optimization, and reinforcement learning. The focus is on how these methods improve domain-specific agent behavior, knowledge use, tool interaction, and task completion.
aspects.bm25_query: domain-specific agents post-training instruction tuning supervised fine-tuning SFT preference optimization DPO reinforcement learning RL agent specialization domain adaptation tool use
aspects.hyde_abstract: General-purpose language models often lack the procedural knowledge, terminology and tool-use skills required for reliable agents in specialized domains. We study post-training methods for building domain-specific agents, comparing supervised fine-tuning, instruction tuning, preference optimization and reinforcement learning from task outcomes. Agents are trained to plan, invoke domain tools, retrieve relevant evidence and complete multi-step workflows using demonstrations, preference comparisons and execution feedback. We evaluate across scientific, software engineering, legal and healthcare environments using task success, factuality, tool-call accuracy, constraint satisfaction and human judgments. Supervised fine-tuning improves basic workflow execution, while preference optimization better aligns responses with domain conventions. Reinforcement learning provides the largest gains on long-horizon tasks with verifiable outcomes, but is sensitive to reward design and simulator quality. Results show that effective post-training depends on matching the learning signal to the domain agent’s interaction structure.

question: How are LLMs used to generate political stories or narratives, and how is their capability evaluated?

aspects.name: LLM political narrative generation
aspects.description: Papers that use large language models (LLMs) to generate political stories, narratives, or other politically themed text. This includes narrative generation for political communication, news, campaigns, persuasion, and public discourse.
aspects.bm25_query: LLM large language model political narrative story generation political communication campaign discourse news persuasion propaganda synthetic media storytelling
aspects.hyde_abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to generate political stories and narratives, yet their effects on political communication remain poorly understood. We study how instruction-tuned LLMs produce narratives about elections, political actors, policy issues, and social groups under prompts that vary in framing, ideology, emotional tone, and target audience. We compare open and proprietary systems across free-form storytelling, news-style reporting, campaign messaging, and persuasive narratives. Generated texts are analyzed for topical coherence, political framing, sentiment, moral language, factuality, and persuasive appeal using human annotation and automated classifiers. LLMs produce fluent and internally coherent narratives, but their outputs exhibit systematic sensitivity to prompt framing and audience specification. We also find recurring tendencies toward generic political tropes, uneven representation of actors, and unsupported claims, highlighting the need for careful oversight of political narrative generation.

aspects.name: Evaluating political narratives
aspects.description: Papers that evaluate the capability of LLMs to generate political stories or narratives, including quality, coherence, factuality, framing, bias, persuasion, and ideological consistency.
aspects.bm25_query: LLM large language model political narrative story generation evaluation factuality coherence framing bias ideology persuasion fluency human annotation
aspects.hyde_abstract: Evaluating LLM-generated political narratives requires measuring more than grammatical fluency. We propose a multidimensional framework for assessing stories and narratives about political events, candidates, parties, and policies. The framework combines human judgments of coherence, relevance, plausibility, factual accuracy, ideological framing, emotional appeal, and persuasive effectiveness with automatic measures of semantic consistency and claim verification. We apply it to narratives generated under controlled prompts and compare expert annotators with general-audience raters and language-model judges. Human and automatic scores agree moderately on surface quality but diverge substantially on factuality, ideological slant, and persuasion. Models that generate the most fluent narratives do not consistently produce the most accurate or balanced accounts. Our findings support reporting separate capability dimensions rather than relying on a single quality score for political story generation.

question: How do we measure whether stories can be linked back to real individuals or leak private information, and what methods reduce this re-identification risk?

aspects.name: Measuring story re-identification risk
aspects.description: Papers that measure whether narrative stories can be linked to real individuals, including identity disclosure, attribute inference, and membership or record linkage from textual details. The focus is on risk assessment for stories and narrative text containing potentially identifying information.
aspects.bm25_query: stories narratives re-identification identity disclosure privacy leakage record linkage entity resolution author identification attribute inference quasi-identifiers PII personally identifiable information
aspects.hyde_abstract: Narrative text often contains combinations of occupations, locations, events, relationships, and temporal details that can identify individuals even after names are removed. We study how to measure re-identification risk in stories by comparing narratives against auxiliary records and testing whether human annotators or language models can recover the underlying person. We evaluate exact identity matching, top-k entity retrieval, attribute inference, and disclosure of sensitive properties under different levels of background knowledge. Results show that seemingly innocuous details become identifying when combined, particularly for rare events and distinctive life histories. Surface-level removal of names provides limited protection, while risk estimates based on uniqueness, linkage success, and inferred sensitive attributes give a more reliable account of privacy leakage. We recommend reporting both adversarial re-identification accuracy and calibrated disclosure risk across demographic groups.

aspects.name: Reducing story privacy risk
aspects.description: Papers that reduce the risk of linking stories to real individuals or extracting private information, using de-identification, anonymization, rewriting, obfuscation, synthetic data, or privacy-preserving generation. Methods should preserve narrative utility while limiting identity disclosure and sensitive-attribute leakage.
aspects.bm25_query: stories narratives privacy-preserving de-identification anonymization redaction pseudonymization paraphrasing obfuscation differential privacy synthetic text re-identification
aspects.hyde_abstract: We investigate methods for reducing re-identification and private-information leakage in narrative stories while preserving their usefulness for research and communication. Our pipeline detects names, locations, dates, relationships, and rare biographical details, then applies entity replacement, controlled rewriting, detail generalization, or synthetic story generation. We evaluate the resulting texts using automated linkage attacks, human identification studies, sensitive-attribute inference, privacy risk measures, and semantic and narrative utility metrics. Replacing explicit identifiers reduces direct disclosure, but attackers still exploit distinctive combinations of facts and stylistic clues. Controlled abstraction and targeted rewriting provide a better privacy-utility trade-off than indiscriminate deletion, while fully synthetic stories offer the strongest protection at the cost of factual fidelity. We also show that privacy auditing must be repeated after generation because fluent rewrites can introduce new identifying details.

question: How can knowledge graphs be combined with LLMs to answer complex multi-hop questions?

aspects.name: Knowledge-graph LLM integration
aspects.description: Papers that combine knowledge graphs with large language models (LLMs) to answer complex multi-hop questions. This includes architectures that retrieve, inject, verbalize, or otherwise represent graph knowledge during question answering.
aspects.bm25_query: knowledge graph KG large language model LLM multi-hop question answering QA graph retrieval graph-augmented generation entity relations reasoning
aspects.hyde_abstract: Large language models often struggle with complex questions that require retrieving and composing facts across multiple entities and relations. We study knowledge-graph-augmented question answering, in which a language model accesses a structured graph during inference and uses the retrieved subgraph to generate an answer. Our system identifies entities in the question, expands relevant neighbors, ranks candidate paths, and verbalizes the resulting evidence as context for the model. We compare direct graph retrieval, graph encodings, and natural-language subgraph descriptions on multi-hop question-answering datasets. Graph grounding improves exact match and answer attribution, particularly for questions requiring three or more reasoning steps, while unrestricted retrieval introduces distractors. Ablation results show that entity linking and path selection are more important than simply increasing the number of retrieved triples.

aspects.name: Multi-hop graph reasoning
aspects.description: Papers that develop reasoning strategies for LLMs answering multi-hop questions over knowledge graphs, including path traversal, relation composition, iterative retrieval, and graph-aware inference.
aspects.bm25_query: knowledge graph LLM multi-hop reasoning question answering relational path traversal relation composition iterative retrieval graph neural network chain reasoning
aspects.hyde_abstract: Answering multi-hop questions over a knowledge graph requires more than retrieving isolated supporting facts: a system must identify a sequence of relations and compose them correctly. We propose an iterative reasoning framework in which an LLM selects entities and relations, traverses the graph, and updates its intermediate hypothesis after each hop. The framework combines constrained candidate generation with graph-aware reranking and asks the model to produce an explicit evidence path before writing the final answer. On compositional question-answering tasks, it reduces reasoning errors and improves evidence recall compared with single-step graph retrieval and unconstrained chain-of-thought prompting. Detailed analysis shows that most failures arise from ambiguous entity resolution, branching subgraphs, and incorrect stopping decisions. The results demonstrate that structured traversal can make LLM reasoning more reliable and interpretable.

aspects.name: Grounded answer verification
aspects.description: Papers that improve the reliability of LLM answers to complex multi-hop questions by verifying generated claims against knowledge-graph evidence, detecting unsupported reasoning, and measuring faithfulness.
aspects.bm25_query: knowledge graph LLM multi-hop question answering verification factuality faithfulness evidence attribution hallucination consistency answer validation
aspects.hyde_abstract: Knowledge-graph augmentation can provide evidence for multi-hop question answering, but language models may still generate answers that are inconsistent with the retrieved facts or unsupported by the inferred path. We introduce a verification pipeline that decomposes an answer into claims, maps each claim to graph triples, and checks whether the proposed relation chain entails the response. We evaluate answer accuracy, evidence recall, citation correctness, and hallucination rate across questions with varying hop counts and graph ambiguity. Verification improves factual precision and identifies unsupported answers that conventional exact-match scoring misses. However, strict graph consistency can reject valid answers when the knowledge graph is incomplete. Our findings support joint reporting of answer correctness and evidence-grounding quality for graph-augmented LLM question answering.

question: What recent techniques improve knowledge distillation from large to small language models?

aspects.name: Distillation techniques for language models
aspects.description: Papers that develop recent techniques for transferring knowledge from large language models to smaller language models through teacher supervision, distillation objectives, or improved training signals.
aspects.bm25_query: knowledge distillation language models LLM teacher student large small compact model logits soft labels response distillation objective
aspects.hyde_abstract: Knowledge distillation is an effective way to transfer the capabilities of large language models to smaller, less expensive models, but conventional next-token distillation often provides limited gains. We study recent distillation techniques that improve the training signal, including soft-label supervision, temperature scaling, teacher-generated responses, intermediate representations and adaptive weighting of difficult tokens. We compare these techniques across instruction following, knowledge-intensive question answering, reasoning and generation tasks, controlling for student size, training data and compute. The experiments show that combining teacher responses with token-level distribution matching consistently outperforms supervised fine-tuning and standard hard-label distillation. Intermediate-layer alignment is most useful when teacher and student architectures are compatible, whereas adaptive objectives provide larger gains for heterogeneous model pairs. Analysis indicates that improved distillation mainly comes from preserving uncertainty and informative alternative continuations.

aspects.name: Data and response generation
aspects.description: Papers that improve knowledge distillation from large to small language models by selecting, synthesizing, filtering, or augmenting the data and teacher responses used for student training.
aspects.bm25_query: knowledge distillation language models data selection synthetic data teacher-generated responses instruction tuning filtering curriculum self-instruct large teacher small student
aspects.hyde_abstract: The quality and diversity of distillation data strongly constrain how well a small language model can inherit the abilities of a large teacher. We investigate data-centric techniques for large-to-small language model distillation, including teacher-generated instruction-response pairs, targeted sampling, difficulty-aware curricula, response filtering and diversity-based deduplication. Rather than distilling on randomly collected prompts, we construct mixtures that emphasize reasoning, factual recall, dialogue and long-tail capabilities, while removing low-confidence or repetitive teacher outputs. Across several student architectures and parameter scales, targeted synthetic data improves instruction following and factual accuracy more reliably than simply increasing the number of examples. Difficulty-aware curricula are especially beneficial for reasoning tasks, but excessive filtering reduces coverage. Our findings show that prompt diversity, teacher confidence and capability-balanced sampling are important design variables for effective distillation.

aspects.name: Reasoning and process distillation
aspects.description: Papers that transfer multi-step reasoning abilities from large to small language models by distilling rationales, intermediate steps, critiques, tool traces, or other process-level supervision.
aspects.bm25_query: reasoning distillation language models rationale chain-of-thought process supervision intermediate reasoning traces critique tool-use student teacher small model
aspects.hyde_abstract: Small language models frequently imitate final answers from large teachers without acquiring the reasoning abilities needed to solve unfamiliar problems. We study process-level distillation, in which teachers provide rationales, decompositions, self-corrections, critiques or tool-use traces in addition to final outputs. Students are trained with objectives that selectively preserve useful intermediate states while avoiding dependence on verbose or unfaithful explanations. On mathematical reasoning, multi-hop question answering and symbolic tasks, process distillation improves generalization over answer-only distillation, particularly when the student has limited capacity. Automatically verified traces are more valuable than unrestricted chain-of-thought, and concise structured plans outperform lengthy explanations in several settings. Ablations show that filtering incorrect intermediate steps and matching the process format to the student are critical for transferring reasoning rather than merely memorizing teacher answers.

aspects.name: Efficient and adaptive distillation
aspects.description: Papers that make large-to-small language model distillation more effective or affordable through adaptive teacher supervision, selective token or layer matching, architecture-aware transfer, and compute-efficient training.
aspects.bm25_query: efficient knowledge distillation language models adaptive distillation selective tokens layer alignment architecture mismatch compute-efficient teacher student compression pruning quantization
aspects.hyde_abstract: Distilling a small language model from a large teacher can require substantial teacher inference and student training compute, especially for long sequences and mismatched architectures. We propose efficient distillation strategies that adapt supervision to the example, token and layer: easy tokens receive inexpensive targets, uncertain regions receive richer teacher distributions, and hidden-state alignment is applied only to compatible representations. We also examine teacher caching, selective response generation and joint distillation with pruning or quantization. Across multiple student sizes, adaptive supervision achieves similar or better quality than full token-level distillation while reducing teacher calls and training cost. The largest savings occur when examples contain long predictable spans. Architecture-aware transfer is important for heterogeneous teacher-student pairs, where indiscriminate layer matching can hurt generation quality. These results suggest that distillation budgets should focus on uncertain and capability-critical content.

question: How reliable are LLMs as automatic evaluators of generated text

aspects.name: LLM-based text evaluation
aspects.description: Papers that assess how reliably large language models (LLMs) can automatically evaluate generated text, including their agreement with human judgments across quality dimensions such as correctness, relevance, coherence, fluency, and helpfulness.
aspects.bm25_query: LLM large language model automatic evaluation generated text evaluator judge text quality human judgments agreement reliability rubric coherence relevance fluency helpfulness
aspects.hyde_abstract: Large language models are increasingly used as automatic evaluators of generated text, but their judgments may not consistently reflect human assessments. We conduct a systematic study of LLM-based evaluation across summarization, dialogue, translation, and open-ended generation, measuring agreement with expert and crowd-sourced ratings for relevance, factuality, coherence, fluency, and helpfulness. We compare pointwise scoring, pairwise preference judgments, and rubric-based evaluation across several model families and prompt designs. LLM evaluators show strong agreement on broad quality differences but are less reliable for subtle factual errors, stylistic distinctions, and borderline cases. Reliability improves with explicit criteria, structured outputs, and multiple judging samples, although model-generated scores remain sensitive to prompt wording and candidate presentation order. Our findings identify when LLM judges provide a useful substitute for human evaluation and when human assessment remains necessary.

question: When should LLM systems rely on long-context models versus retrieval-augmented generation or explicit memory mechanisms?

aspects.name: Long-context LLM systems
aspects.description: Papers that use long-context language models to handle extensive documents, conversation histories, or persistent information without external retrieval or memory modules. They study the conditions under which increasing the context window improves LLM system quality and practicality.
aspects.bm25_query: LLM long-context language models extended context window long-context modeling lengthy documents conversation history needle-in-a-haystack context utilization distraction inference cost
aspects.hyde_abstract: Long-context language models provide a simple alternative to external retrieval and memory by placing large amounts of information directly in the prompt. We study when this strategy is effective for LLM systems that answer questions over lengthy documents and maintain extended conversational histories. We vary context length, information density, evidence position and distractor content, and compare full-context prompting with shorter contexts containing only relevant information. Long-context models perform well when evidence is dense, references are distributed across the input, or reasoning requires global document structure. However, accuracy declines when relevant evidence is sparse, repeated distractors increase attention demands, and inference cost becomes substantial. Our analysis shows that nominal context-window size is a poor proxy for usable context and identifies workload characteristics favoring direct long-context processing.

aspects.name: Retrieval-augmented generation
aspects.description: Papers that use retrieval-augmented generation to supply LLM systems with relevant external information instead of placing all available information in the context. They examine when retrieval improves answer quality, efficiency, factuality, and adaptation to changing knowledge.
aspects.bm25_query: retrieval-augmented generation RAG LLM retrieval dense retriever reranking document question answering external knowledge context selection factuality latency
aspects.hyde_abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation reduces the input burden on LLM systems by selecting a small set of passages from a larger corpus before generation. We investigate when RAG is preferable to processing an entire source collection with a long-context model. Across document question answering, knowledge-intensive dialogue and temporally changing information, retrieval improves efficiency and factuality when relevant evidence is sparse and the corpus is large. Its benefits diminish when questions require synthesis across many dispersed passages or when the retriever fails to identify the needed evidence. We compare dense retrieval, hybrid search and reranking under fixed latency budgets. Results show that retrieval quality and evidence coverage, rather than context-window length alone, determine the usefulness of RAG, while retrieval errors remain its dominant failure mode.

aspects.name: Explicit memory mechanisms
aspects.description: Papers that equip LLM systems with explicit memory mechanisms, such as structured memories, episodic memories, summaries, or external stores, to retain information across interactions or tasks. They study when persistent memory is preferable to repeatedly using long contexts or retrieving from an unstructured corpus.
aspects.bm25_query: LLM memory external memory episodic memory conversational memory persistent memory memory management summarization structured memory long-term dialogue personalization
aspects.hyde_abstract: Explicit memory mechanisms allow LLM systems to retain and organize information across interactions rather than repeatedly processing complete conversation histories. We study episodic memories, compressed summaries and structured user profiles for long-term dialogue and personalized assistance. The system extracts candidate memories, assigns provenance and recency metadata, and retrieves or updates them when future turns require prior information. Compared with unrestricted conversation-history prompting and document retrieval, explicit memory improves consistency on recurring preferences and enables lower inference cost over long sessions. Its weaknesses include incorrect memory formation, stale facts and unwanted retention of irrelevant or sensitive details. Evaluations measuring recall, contradiction rate, personalization and memory-editing behavior show that explicit memory is most useful for persistent, user-specific information rather than one-off factual questions.

aspects.name: Choosing context strategies
aspects.description: Papers that directly compare long-context models, retrieval-augmented generation, and explicit memory mechanisms for LLM systems. They identify workload, evidence, latency, cost, update frequency, and persistence conditions that determine when each strategy should be used.
aspects.bm25_query: long-context RAG retrieval-augmented generation explicit memory LLM comparison context window trade-offs latency cost evidence persistence hybrid systems
aspects.hyde_abstract: LLM system designers must choose among long-context processing, retrieval-augmented generation and explicit memory, yet these mechanisms are often evaluated in isolation. We present a controlled comparison across workloads differing in corpus size, evidence dispersion, update frequency, session length and personalization requirements. Long-context models are strongest when the relevant information is distributed throughout a moderate-sized source and global interactions matter. RAG offers the best cost-quality trade-off for large, searchable and frequently updated collections, but suffers from retrieval misses. Explicit memory is superior for stable user-specific information that must persist across sessions, while requiring safeguards against stale or incorrect memories. Hybrid systems that retrieve documents and maintain compact memories perform best overall, suggesting that strategy selection should be based on information structure rather than context-window capacity alone.

question: What does it take to train an LLM agent that calls external APIs reliably?

aspects.name: Training API-calling agents
aspects.description: Papers on training LLM agents to reliably invoke external APIs, including learning when to call, which endpoint to select, and how to produce valid arguments. The focus is on tool-using agents whose actions depend on API specifications and execution feedback.
aspects.bm25_query: LLM agent tool-using API calling function calling tool learning endpoint selection argument generation API schema training
aspects.hyde_abstract: Large language model agents increasingly interact with external services through APIs, but reliable tool use requires more than generating syntactically plausible calls. We study training procedures that teach agents to select the appropriate endpoint, construct schema-valid arguments, and decide when an API call is necessary. Our approach combines supervised trajectories with execution-aware preference optimization, using API responses and structured error messages to improve subsequent actions. We evaluate on diverse APIs involving search, databases, calendars, payments, and code execution, measuring call accuracy, argument validity, task completion, and the number of failed requests. Training with realistic tool documentation and both successful and erroneous executions substantially improves reliability, especially for long-horizon tasks. Ablations show that endpoint selection and argument grounding remain the primary sources of failure, while execution feedback reduces repeated invalid calls.

aspects.name: Reliable API execution
aspects.description: Papers that address the operational reliability of LLM agents calling external APIs, including error handling, retries, authentication, rate limits, malformed requests, and recovery from failed tool calls. These studies evaluate whether agents complete tasks robustly under realistic API conditions rather than only producing valid-looking calls.
aspects.bm25_query: LLM agent API reliability tool use error handling retry recovery malformed requests rate limits authentication timeout execution feedback
aspects.hyde_abstract: External APIs introduce failures that are absent from static language-model benchmarks, including authentication errors, rate limits, timeouts, invalid parameters, and inconsistent responses. We present a reliability framework for LLM agents that combines typed tool interfaces, explicit error classification, bounded retries, and recovery policies conditioned on execution feedback. The agent distinguishes correctable argument errors from transient service failures and escalates irrecoverable cases instead of repeatedly issuing harmful requests. We evaluate on simulated and live API environments with injected faults, reporting task success, valid-call rate, recovery rate, request cost, latency, and unsafe duplicate actions. Compared with unconstrained tool calling, structured error handling improves completion under fault conditions and substantially reduces repeated invalid requests, while calibrated stopping is essential for controlling latency and side effects.

aspects.name: API grounding and planning
aspects.description: Papers on how API documentation, tool schemas, retrieval, and multi-step planning support reliable API use by LLM agents. The core concern is grounding decisions and arguments in available endpoints, constraints, dependencies, and returned results.
aspects.bm25_query: LLM agent API documentation tool schema retrieval planning multi-step tool use function calling parameter grounding dependency execution trace
aspects.hyde_abstract: Reliable API use depends on grounding agent decisions in changing documentation, endpoint constraints, and the outputs of earlier calls. We investigate an agent architecture that retrieves relevant API specifications, represents parameter dependencies explicitly, and plans multi-step interactions before execution while revising the plan after each response. Tool schemas are normalized into typed descriptions containing required fields, admissible values, authentication requirements, and side-effect warnings. On compositional tasks requiring several dependent API calls, schema retrieval and execution-conditioned replanning improve endpoint selection and argument accuracy over prompting with raw documentation alone. We evaluate plan validity, call-level precision, task completion, latency, and robustness to ambiguous or outdated documentation. Results show that planning helps mainly when dependencies span multiple services, whereas retrieval is most valuable for large and evolving tool inventories.

aspects.name: Evaluating API agent reliability
aspects.description: Papers that define benchmarks, metrics, and experimental protocols for measuring the reliability of LLM agents that call external APIs. Relevant work tests correctness, robustness, safety, cost, and consistency across varied tools and failure conditions.
aspects.bm25_query: LLM agent API tool-use evaluation benchmark reliability function calling task success argument validity robustness safety latency cost
aspects.hyde_abstract: Existing evaluations of tool-using language models often count whether an agent eventually answers a question, overlooking invalid calls, unnecessary requests, unsafe side effects, and recovery behavior. We introduce an evaluation protocol for API-calling agents that reports endpoint-selection accuracy, schema-valid argument rate, execution success, task completion, recovery after injected failures, duplicate-call rate, latency, token usage, and cost. The protocol covers single-step and long-horizon tasks across read-only and state-changing APIs, with controlled variation in documentation quality, authorization, rate limits, and response formats. We find that answer accuracy can conceal substantial operational unreliability: agents frequently complete tasks after multiple invalid calls or issue redundant side-effecting requests. Reliability profiles and failure taxonomies provide more informative comparisons than aggregate success alone.

question: How can a chatbot be stopped from agreeing with users who are wrong?

aspects.name: Reducing chatbot sycophancy
aspects.description: Papers that study how chatbots can avoid agreeing with users when the user's claim, premise, or reasoning is incorrect. This includes sycophancy detection, factual correction, uncertainty communication, and training or prompting interventions that encourage appropriate disagreement.
aspects.bm25_query: chatbot sycophancy user disagreement incorrect claims factual correction truthfulness alignment preference optimization RLHF hallucination uncertainty calibration
aspects.hyde_abstract: Chatbots frequently endorse users’ incorrect claims, creating a form of sycophancy that undermines factual reliability and user trust. We study methods for encouraging appropriate disagreement while preserving helpfulness and conversational rapport. We construct conversations containing false premises, leading questions, and unsupported user opinions, and compare supervised fine-tuning, preference optimization, critique prompting, retrieval augmentation, and uncertainty-aware response generation. Systems are evaluated for factual accuracy, contradiction of false claims, calibrated uncertainty, politeness, and resistance to user pressure. Training on contrastive examples that distinguish agreement from justified acknowledgment substantially reduces sycophantic responses, while retrieval improves correction of externally verifiable claims. However, aggressive contradiction increases false refusals and harms subjective or ambiguous discussions. The best systems explicitly explain the evidence, state uncertainty, and distinguish factual correction from disagreement about values.

question: How would you build a strong language model for a language with almost no digital text?

aspects.name: Data creation for extremely low-resource languages
aspects.description: Papers on building a strong language model for a language with almost no digital text by creating, collecting, digitizing, or augmenting scarce text and speech data. This includes web mining, transcription, translation, synthetic data, and community-centered data collection.
aspects.bm25_query: extremely low-resource language scarce text data collection corpus creation web mining digitization transcription speech translation synthetic data documentation
aspects.hyde_abstract: Languages with almost no digital text remain poorly represented in contemporary language modeling, largely because standard web-scale pretraining is impossible. We study a data creation pipeline for extremely low-resource languages that combines community transcription, optical character recognition, speech recognition, targeted web mining, bilingual translation, and controlled synthetic text generation. We measure the effects of each source on corpus size, linguistic diversity, contamination, and downstream model quality. Experiments show that carefully filtered translated and transcribed text provides larger gains than unfiltered synthetic expansion, while community-produced material improves coverage of local entities and styles. Deduplication, provenance tracking, and native-speaker validation are essential for preventing noisy or culturally inappropriate data from dominating the corpus. The resulting pipeline substantially improves language modeling and basic generation despite using orders of magnitude less text than typical pretraining corpora.

aspects.name: Cross-lingual transfer and multilingual pretraining
aspects.description: Papers on building a strong model for an almost-undigitized language by transferring knowledge from related, typologically similar, or geographically connected languages. Relevant work includes multilingual pretraining, continued pretraining, adapters, parameter sharing, and cross-lingual transfer.
aspects.bm25_query: extremely low-resource language multilingual pretraining cross-lingual transfer related languages typological similarity continued pretraining adapters parameter sharing
aspects.hyde_abstract: For languages with almost no digital text, a model must acquire much of its linguistic knowledge from other languages. We investigate multilingual pretraining and continued pretraining strategies that transfer representations from genealogically related and typologically similar languages into an extremely low-resource target language. We compare shared multilingual vocabularies, language-specific adapters, vocabulary expansion, parameter-efficient continued pretraining, and mixture reweighting using only a small target-language corpus. Transfer from related languages improves morphology and syntax, but unrelated high-resource languages contribute useful semantic and factual knowledge. The strongest system combines multilingual initialization with target-language continued pretraining and adapter-based specialization. We further show that language similarity alone is insufficient: script, tokenization efficiency, domain overlap, and orthographic consistency are important predictors of transfer quality.

aspects.name: Tokenization and model architecture
aspects.description: Papers on designing the tokenizer, vocabulary, model size, and architecture for a strong language model when the target language has extremely little text. The focus is on avoiding poor segmentation and making scarce training examples more informative.
aspects.bm25_query: extremely low-resource language tokenizer vocabulary subword segmentation character byte-level morphology script tokenization efficiency architecture
aspects.hyde_abstract: Subword tokenizers trained on dominant languages often represent extremely low-resource languages inefficiently, producing long sequences and fragmenting morphologically meaningful units. We examine byte-level, character-level, multilingual subword, and target-language-adapted tokenization for language modeling with very limited text. We evaluate fertility, sequence length, rare-word coverage, morphological consistency, memory use, and downstream generation quality after multilingual initialization. Target-language vocabulary expansion reduces fragmentation, while character and byte representations provide robustness when orthographic data are scarce. However, indiscriminate vocabulary growth increases embedding parameters and can reduce transfer from the multilingual base model. A hybrid tokenizer with reserved capacity for the target language and shared units for related languages offers the best trade-off, particularly for inflection-rich languages and scripts underrepresented in the pretraining corpus.

aspects.name: Training and adaptation with scarce data
aspects.description: Papers on efficiently adapting a pretrained language model to an almost-undigitized language while preventing overfitting and catastrophic forgetting. This covers continued pretraining, parameter-efficient tuning, curriculum design, regularization, and data mixing.
aspects.bm25_query: extremely low-resource language continued pretraining parameter-efficient fine-tuning PEFT adapters LoRA catastrophic forgetting overfitting data mixing curriculum
aspects.hyde_abstract: Adapting a pretrained multilingual model to a language with almost no digital text is constrained by overfitting, unstable optimization, and catastrophic forgetting of transferred knowledge. We compare full continued pretraining with adapters, low-rank adaptation, prompt tuning, and mixed-language training under fixed target-language data budgets. We vary sampling temperature, replay of related-language data, sequence packing, curriculum order, and regularization strength. Parameter-efficient adaptation consistently outperforms unrestricted updates when the target corpus is small, while replay preserves multilingual capabilities and improves generalization beyond memorized passages. The best configuration begins with broad multilingual transfer, gradually increases target-language sampling, and evaluates on held-out speakers, domains, and topics. Results show that training strategy can matter as much as corpus size in ultra-low-resource language modeling.

aspects.name: Evaluation and community validation
aspects.description: Papers on assessing whether a model built for a language with almost no digital text is genuinely strong, useful, and safe. This includes intrinsic language modeling metrics, human evaluation, culturally relevant tasks, robustness, documentation, and native-speaker participation.
aspects.bm25_query: extremely low-resource language model evaluation perplexity generation human evaluation native speakers cultural safety documentation robustness benchmark
aspects.hyde_abstract: Standard multilingual benchmarks provide little evidence about whether a model works for a language with almost no digital text. We develop an evaluation framework combining held-out perplexity, morphology-sensitive prediction, translation, question answering, summarization, speech-text interaction, and open-ended generation. Native speakers assess fluency, grammaticality, factuality, dialect coverage, cultural appropriateness, and harmful fabrication using locally developed prompts and rubrics. We also test robustness to spelling variation, code-switching, orthographic inconsistency, and distribution shift across speakers and domains. Automatic metrics correlate weakly with human judgments, especially when reference texts are scarce. We therefore recommend community-led test-set construction, transparent data provenance, explicit reporting of dialect and domain coverage, and evaluation of memorization and consent. These practices reveal improvements hidden by conventional benchmark scores and expose serious failure modes in otherwise fluent systems.

question: Can a teacher reliably tell whether an essay was written by AI?

aspects.name: Teacher detection of AI essays
aspects.description: Papers that study whether teachers, instructors, or other human evaluators can reliably distinguish AI-generated essays from student-written essays. This includes detection accuracy, calibration, false positives, and factors that affect human judgments of authorship.
aspects.bm25_query: AI-generated essays teacher detection human judgment authorship identification educators instructors ChatGPT student writing accuracy reliability false positives
aspects.hyde_abstract: The widespread use of generative language models raises a central question for education: can teachers reliably identify essays written by artificial intelligence? We conduct a controlled study in which teachers classify student essays as human-written or AI-generated, using essays produced by several contemporary language models and essays written by students across academic prompts. We measure accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, confidence calibration and inter-rater agreement, while varying essay quality, revision, prompt type and the availability of contextual information about the student. Teachers perform above chance but substantially below perfect accuracy, with confidence often exceeding correctness. False accusations are more common for multilingual writers and formulaic academic prose, whereas lightly edited AI essays are frequently judged human-written. The findings suggest that unaided teacher judgments are insufficient as definitive evidence of AI authorship and should be combined with process-based writing evidence.

question: How can claims in online news be verified automatically?

aspects.name: Automated news claim verification
aspects.description: Papers that automatically verify factual claims made in online news articles or news-like web content. They study systems that retrieve evidence, assess claim veracity, and predict labels such as supported, refuted, or unverifiable.
aspects.bm25_query: automated news claim verification fact-checking factuality misinformation evidence retrieval entailment stance support refute unverifiable online journalism
aspects.hyde_abstract: Online news contains factual claims that can be difficult to verify at scale, motivating automated fact-checking systems. We study a pipeline that identifies claims in news articles, retrieves evidence from trustworthy web sources, and predicts whether each claim is supported, refuted, or unverifiable. The system combines lexical and semantic retrieval with textual entailment and stance classification, while preserving source provenance for human inspection. We evaluate claim extraction, evidence retrieval, and final veracity prediction separately and end to end on news fact-checking collections containing political, health, and general-interest articles. Results show that evidence retrieval is the main bottleneck: adding diverse sources improves recall but can introduce conflicting or low-quality evidence. The findings support calibrated three-way decisions and abstention when retrieved sources do not provide sufficient justification.

question: How safe are open-weight LLMs against users trying to extract harmful content?

aspects.name: Open-weight extraction safety
aspects.description: Papers that measure how safe open-weight large language models are when users deliberately attempt to extract harmful, dangerous, or otherwise restricted content. This includes direct elicitation, jailbreak prompting, and adversarial misuse of models whose weights are publicly available.
aspects.bm25_query: open-weight open-source LLM large language model harmful content extraction safety jailbreak adversarial prompting red teaming misuse refusal bypass
aspects.hyde_abstract: Open-weight large language models enable transparent research and local deployment, but their accessible parameters may make it easier for users to elicit harmful content. We conduct a systematic red-team study of models released with downloadable weights, evaluating direct requests, jailbreak prompts, multi-turn escalation, role-play, translation, and adversarial reformulations across harmful-content categories. We measure attack success rate, refusal rate, harmfulness of generated responses, and the transferability of attacks across model families and decoding settings. Open-weight models vary substantially in safety: instruction tuning reduces direct compliance, but many models remain vulnerable to adaptive attacks that preserve the user’s harmful intent while avoiding safety keywords. We find that stronger refusal behavior does not always prevent partial assistance, and that local access enables repeated probing and automated attack optimization. Our analysis identifies evaluation practices needed for meaningful open-weight safety comparisons.

question: Whose values do LLMs reflect when answering moral questions in different cultures?

aspects.name: Cultural values in moral answers
aspects.description: Papers that investigate whose moral values large language models reflect when answering moral questions across different cultural, national, religious, or linguistic contexts. This includes measuring cultural alignment, value attribution, and differences between model responses and human moral judgments.
aspects.bm25_query: LLM large language model moral questions ethics values cultural differences cross-cultural moral judgments cultural alignment value pluralism WEIRD nationality religion
aspects.hyde_abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to answer questions involving right and wrong, yet their moral responses may reflect the values of model developers, training data, dominant cultures, or the users who prompt them. We study whose values LLMs express when answering moral questions across culturally diverse populations. We collect parallel moral dilemmas and value-judgment prompts from participants in multiple countries, religions, and linguistic communities, and compare human responses with outputs from several multilingual models. We measure agreement, cultural bias, value attribution, and sensitivity to prompt language and cultural context. Models generally align more closely with high-resource, Western, and English-language judgments than with local responses from underrepresented communities. Explicit cultural framing improves alignment but can produce stereotypes and inconsistent reasoning. Our findings highlight the need for culturally grounded evaluation and transparent reporting of normative assumptions in LLMs.

question: How well can multimodal models read the figures of a scientific paper?

aspects.name: Scientific figure understanding
aspects.description: Papers that measure how well multimodal models interpret figures embedded in scientific papers, including charts, plots, diagrams, tables, and other visualizations. This includes answering questions, extracting information, and recovering the figure’s scientific meaning from its visual and textual context.
aspects.bm25_query: scientific paper figure understanding multimodal large vision-language model chart plot diagram visualization table interpretation question answering OCR caption
aspects.hyde_abstract: Scientific papers communicate essential evidence through figures, yet multimodal models often struggle to interpret plots, diagrams, and complex visualizations reliably. We study the ability of vision-language models to read figures in their surrounding paper context and answer questions about values, trends, comparisons, methods, and conclusions. Our evaluation spans charts, scientific diagrams, tables, and composite figures, with questions requiring visual perception, numerical reasoning, and integration of captions and nearby text. We compare image-only inputs with figure-plus-caption and full-page contexts. Models perform well on direct caption-based questions but make substantial errors when estimating values, resolving legends, tracking multi-panel relationships, or identifying evidence supporting a claim. Detailed error analysis shows that OCR, chart structure recognition, and scientific reasoning remain complementary bottlenecks.

question: What makes step-by-step mathematical reasoning in LLMs trustworthy?

aspects.name: Correct mathematical reasoning
aspects.description: Papers that study when step-by-step mathematical reasoning in large language models is correct, reliable, and robust across problem types, difficulty levels, and distribution shifts. This includes identifying reasoning errors that lead to incorrect final answers.
aspects.bm25_query: chain-of-thought CoT step-by-step mathematical reasoning LLM large language model arithmetic algebra theorem proving correctness reliability robustness reasoning errors
aspects.hyde_abstract: Large language models often produce fluent solutions to mathematical problems, yet their step-by-step reasoning can contain subtle errors that invalidate the final answer. We investigate the conditions under which chain-of-thought reasoning is mathematically correct and robust. We evaluate models on arithmetic, algebra, geometry and theorem-proving problems while varying problem difficulty, numerical representations and distribution shift. Our analysis separates errors in intermediate derivations from errors in the final answer and shows that longer reasoning traces are not necessarily more reliable. Explicit equation checking, decomposition into independently solvable subproblems and consistency across multiple solution paths substantially improve correctness. However, models remain vulnerable to locally plausible algebraic transformations and errors that propagate through later steps. These findings motivate evaluation protocols that verify every intermediate claim rather than reporting final-answer accuracy alone.

aspects.name: Faithful reasoning traces
aspects.description: Papers that examine whether step-by-step mathematical explanations in LLMs faithfully represent the computations and evidence that produced their answers. This aspect covers hidden reasoning, post-hoc rationalizations, and consistency between intermediate steps and final predictions.
aspects.bm25_query: faithful chain-of-thought mathematical reasoning LLM reasoning traces faithfulness process supervision hidden reasoning post-hoc rationalization attribution intermediate steps
aspects.hyde_abstract: Step-by-step mathematical explanations are often treated as evidence that a language model arrived at an answer through valid reasoning, but a generated explanation may instead be a post-hoc rationalization. We study faithfulness in mathematical chain-of-thought by comparing visible reasoning traces with controlled interventions on intermediate steps, alternative solution paths and model-generated answers. We introduce measures of step validity, causal influence and reasoning-answer consistency, and evaluate them on arithmetic, symbolic algebra and word problems. Models frequently produce convincing traces whose individual steps are incomplete or causally unrelated to the final prediction. Training with process-level supervision improves local validity and makes answers more sensitive to corrupted steps, although faithfulness remains imperfect. Our results show that explanation quality and mathematical correctness should be evaluated as separate properties.

aspects.name: Verification and self-correction
aspects.description: Papers that make step-by-step mathematical reasoning in LLMs trustworthy through verifiers, proof checking, execution, self-consistency, critique, or iterative correction. The focus is on mechanisms that detect and repair invalid mathematical reasoning.
aspects.bm25_query: mathematical reasoning LLM verifier verification proof checking process supervision self-consistency self-correction critique chain-of-thought theorem proving error correction
aspects.hyde_abstract: Because language models can generate plausible but invalid mathematical derivations, trustworthy reasoning requires mechanisms that detect and correct errors. We study verifier-guided chain-of-thought for mathematical problem solving, combining candidate solution generation with step-level checking, symbolic calculation and iterative critique. We compare outcome-based reward models, process reward models, self-consistency, external computer algebra systems and formal proof assistants. Step-level verification improves accuracy most when the verifier is sensitive to invalid transformations rather than only the final answer. Self-consistency provides useful redundancy but can amplify shared misconceptions across sampled solutions. On problems requiring multi-step algebraic and deductive reasoning, combining independent candidate generation with executable or formal checks yields the strongest reliability gains. We recommend reporting both final-answer accuracy and the rate at which invalid intermediate reasoning is detected.

question: What is lost when a large language model is compressed to run on a phone?

aspects.name: On-device LLM compression
aspects.description: Papers that study compressing large language models so they can run efficiently on smartphones and other mobile devices. They examine techniques such as quantization, pruning, distillation, and parameter-efficient architectures under phone hardware and memory constraints.
aspects.bm25_query: large language model LLM compression mobile phone smartphone on-device quantization pruning distillation weight sharing memory footprint
aspects.hyde_abstract: Running large language models on smartphones requires substantial reductions in parameter storage, memory use, and computation. We investigate how post-training quantization, structured pruning, knowledge distillation, and weight sharing affect the quality of compact on-device language models. Experiments across instruction following, text generation, question answering, and perplexity tasks show that compression can preserve general linguistic behavior while degrading factual recall, long-context reasoning, and instruction adherence. Weight-only quantization produces the best quality-efficiency trade-off at moderate bit widths, whereas aggressive pruning causes larger losses unless followed by distillation. We additionally measure peak RAM, model size, latency, and energy consumption on representative mobile processors. The results show that the most damaging losses arise when compression reduces activation precision and context capacity, rather than from parameter count alone.

aspects.name: Quality loss under compression
aspects.description: Papers that measure what large language models lose after compression for phone deployment, including knowledge, reasoning, generation quality, robustness, and calibration. This aspect focuses on the behavioral trade-offs between compressed and uncompressed models.
aspects.bm25_query: compressed LLM quality degradation quantization pruning distillation perplexity reasoning factual knowledge instruction following robustness calibration
aspects.hyde_abstract: Compression enables large language models to operate within smartphone resource limits, but aggregate accuracy can obscure important behavioral degradation. We conduct a comprehensive study of compressed models across language modeling, factual knowledge, mathematical reasoning, instruction following, multilingual generation, safety, and calibration. Comparing full-precision models with quantized, pruned, and distilled variants, we find that perplexity changes are weak predictors of downstream losses. Aggressive compression disproportionately harms rare factual knowledge, multi-step reasoning, long-tail languages, and reliable refusal behavior, while common-language generation remains relatively stable. Error rates also increase sharply on long contexts and prompts containing unusual tokens. Our analysis identifies sensitivity to layer depth, activation outliers, and attention projections as major sources of quality loss, suggesting that compression should be evaluated with capability-specific tests rather than a single benchmark score.

aspects.name: Mobile efficiency trade-offs
aspects.description: Papers that jointly evaluate the quality, latency, memory, energy, and privacy trade-offs of compressed large language models running directly on phones. They characterize when quality loss is justified by practical on-device efficiency gains.
aspects.bm25_query: on-device LLM smartphone mobile inference latency energy memory battery efficiency quantization throughput privacy quality trade-off
aspects.hyde_abstract: On-device inference for large language models offers lower latency, offline availability, and improved privacy, but compression introduces capability and systems trade-offs. We evaluate compact language models directly on smartphones under realistic interactive workloads, measuring response quality alongside peak memory, time to first token, generation throughput, energy per query, thermal throttling, and battery consumption. Lower-bit quantization substantially reduces storage and energy, yet memory bandwidth and prompt processing remain bottlenecks for long contexts. Models that appear efficient in desktop benchmarks can become impractical on phones because of sustained power draw and thermal limits. We show that the preferred compression level depends on workload: aggressive compression is suitable for short classification and rewriting requests, while conversational generation benefits from larger, moderately quantized models. We provide deployment guidelines balancing capability, responsiveness, and battery life.

question: Can LLMs replace human participants in social science surveys?

aspects.name: LLMs as survey participants
aspects.description: Papers that investigate whether large language models can serve as substitutes for human participants when answering social science survey questions. This includes eliciting LLM responses, modeling demographic or attitudinal profiles, and comparing synthetic respondents with people.
aspects.bm25_query: LLM large language model synthetic respondents survey participants social science questionnaire human subjects demographic personas attitudes opinions
aspects.hyde_abstract: Large language models are increasingly proposed as inexpensive substitutes for human participants in social science surveys, but their responses may not reflect human attitudes or population diversity. We evaluate language models as synthetic survey respondents by prompting them with demographic profiles, life histories and neutral respondent instructions across political, social and behavioral questionnaires. We compare response distributions, internal consistency and subgroup differences with those of human samples, using agreement, calibration and distributional distance measures. Synthetic respondents reproduce broad associations found in human data but show reduced variance, exaggerated normativity and sensitivity to prompt wording. Persona conditioning recovers some demographic variation, yet does not reliably reproduce intersectional patterns or minority viewpoints. These findings suggest that LLMs can support piloting and hypothesis generation, but should not replace human participants for estimating population beliefs.

aspects.name: Validity of synthetic survey data
aspects.description: Papers that assess the reliability, validity and representativeness of LLM-generated responses in social science surveys. The focus is whether synthetic responses support valid population-level inference rather than merely resembling individual human answers.
aspects.bm25_query: LLM synthetic data survey validity reliability representativeness social science population inference response distributions human comparison measurement bias calibration
aspects.hyde_abstract: Synthetic survey responses from large language models could reduce the cost of social science research, but their usefulness depends on whether they preserve measurement and population properties of human data. We develop a validation framework comparing LLM-generated and human responses across attitude scales, factual beliefs and behavioral intentions. The analysis examines response distributions, reliability, construct validity, subgroup representation, test-retest stability and sensitivity to sampling and prompting choices. LLM responses often achieve high item-level agreement while producing distorted marginal distributions and stronger correlations between related constructs than human respondents. Demographic prompting improves some subgroup contrasts but cannot guarantee representative sampling or valid uncertainty estimates. We conclude that synthetic data should be treated as a model-dependent simulation requiring external human validation, not as direct evidence of public opinion.

aspects.name: Human versus LLM responses
aspects.description: Papers that directly compare LLM survey participants with human participants, including experiments on agreement, bias, heterogeneity, reasoning, and response behavior in social science questionnaires.
aspects.bm25_query: human LLM comparison survey respondents social science questionnaire agreement heterogeneity bias response behavior experimental study
aspects.hyde_abstract: We conduct a controlled comparison of human and large language model respondents on a diverse set of social science survey instruments. Models answer the same questions under standardized instructions, with and without demographic personas, while human participants complete the questionnaires under matched conditions. We compare answer frequencies, scale reliability, response times, straightlining, acquiescence, sensitivity to question order and correlations with demographic characteristics. LLMs show greater consistency and lower random error than humans, but they also exhibit reduced response heterogeneity, weaker effects of personal experience and systematic alignment with socially desirable answers. Persona prompts create apparent subgroup differences that are unstable across model families and decoding settings. Direct agreement with aggregate human results therefore overstates the evidential equivalence of synthetic and human participants.

question: How much can we trust the leaderboard scores of modern LLMs?

aspects.name: Reliability of LLM leaderboards
aspects.description: Papers that assess how trustworthy leaderboard scores are as estimates of modern large language model capability. This includes score validity, reproducibility, and whether rankings remain meaningful across evaluation settings.
aspects.bm25_query: LLM large language model leaderboard score reliability validity reproducibility ranking benchmark evaluation capability
aspects.hyde_abstract: Leaderboards are widely used to summarize the capabilities of modern large language models, yet their scores may not provide stable or comparable estimates of quality. We study leaderboard reliability by analyzing benchmark construction, model submissions, scoring procedures, and ranking uncertainty across multiple evaluation settings. We distinguish measurement error, sampling variance, and systematic sources of bias, including contamination, prompt sensitivity, and selective reporting. Repeated evaluations reveal that small score differences often do not support confident claims about model ordering, while rankings can change substantially under alternative prompts, aggregations, and random seeds. We recommend reporting confidence intervals, paired statistical tests, evaluation protocols, and sensitivity analyses rather than single aggregate scores. Our findings show that leaderboard results are useful signals of capability, but substantially less trustworthy as precise rankings of modern LLMs.

aspects.name: Benchmark contamination and gaming
aspects.description: Papers that examine whether modern LLM leaderboard scores are inflated by training-data contamination, benchmark leakage, adaptive behavior, or optimization against public evaluation sets. The focus is how these factors undermine trust in leaderboard scores.
aspects.bm25_query: LLM large language model leaderboard benchmark contamination data leakage memorization test set leakage gaming overfitting evaluation
aspects.hyde_abstract: Public benchmarks create incentives for developers to optimize models and prompts for leaderboard performance, raising concerns about contamination and evaluation gaming. We investigate whether modern large language models have encountered benchmark items during pretraining, instruction tuning, or post-training, and whether this exposure inflates leaderboard scores. We combine dataset provenance analysis, memorization probes, paraphrased test items, and temporally held-out evaluation. Models with apparent state-of-the-art results often lose substantially more accuracy on private or newly generated items than on public test sets, especially when benchmark examples are widely circulated. We further show that prompt engineering and submission-specific tuning can produce leaderboard gains without corresponding improvements in general capability. These findings motivate contamination audits and continuously refreshed, hidden evaluations.

aspects.name: Robustness of leaderboard rankings
aspects.description: Papers that test whether modern LLM leaderboard rankings are robust to changes in prompts, judges, tasks, datasets, seeds, and aggregation methods. They quantify uncertainty and rank reversals in leaderboard-based comparisons.
aspects.bm25_query: LLM leaderboard ranking robustness rank instability prompt sensitivity judge variance confidence intervals statistical significance benchmark aggregation
aspects.hyde_abstract: Leaderboard rankings for large language models are often interpreted as precise orderings, although evaluations involve substantial design choices and stochasticity. We perform a robustness analysis that varies prompts, decoding settings, judge models, task subsets, random seeds, and score aggregation rules. Across representative benchmarks, model rankings exhibit frequent reversals when score gaps are small, and pairwise preferences are especially sensitive to evaluator choice and prompt wording. Bootstrap confidence intervals and hierarchical models show that many published improvements are not statistically distinguishable. We propose reporting rank distributions and pairwise win probabilities instead of a single ordinal leaderboard. The results demonstrate that leaderboard conclusions should be framed as uncertainty-aware comparisons, with claims restricted to differences that persist across evaluation protocols.

question: What is the best way to build a voice assistant on top of language models?

aspects.name: Speech-language interface
aspects.description: Papers on building voice assistants on top of language models by connecting automatic speech recognition and text-to-speech with the language-model dialogue system. They study robustness to noisy speech, turn-taking, interruption, prosody and end-to-end spoken interaction.
aspects.bm25_query: voice assistant speech-to-speech automatic speech recognition ASR text-to-speech TTS spoken dialogue language model turn-taking interruption noise prosody
aspects.hyde_abstract: Voice assistants built on language models must transform spontaneous speech into reliable textual or acoustic representations while preserving conversational timing. We present a modular spoken-dialogue architecture that combines streaming automatic speech recognition, a language-model dialogue controller, and incremental text-to-speech synthesis. The system detects endpointing, supports barge-in interruptions, and uses prosodic cues to improve turn-taking. We evaluate recognition quality, response latency, interruption recovery, dialogue success, and user satisfaction under background noise and disfluent speech. Compared with a batch pipeline, streaming inference reduces perceived latency and improves conversational naturalness, while endpointing errors remain the main source of failed interactions. The findings show that robust speech interfaces require joint optimization of transcription, turn management, and speech generation rather than simply wrapping a text chatbot with audio components.

aspects.name: Language-model assistant architecture
aspects.description: Papers on how to architect voice assistants around language models, including dialogue state, tool use, memory, planning, grounding and safety. The focus is on reliable task completion in spoken interaction rather than general language-model agents.
aspects.bm25_query: voice assistant language model dialogue management conversational agent tool use function calling memory grounding planning task-oriented spoken dialogue safety
aspects.hyde_abstract: Language models provide flexible dialogue capabilities, but voice assistants must also maintain state, invoke tools, ground responses in external information, and recover from misunderstandings. We develop a voice-assistant architecture in which a language model performs dialogue-state tracking and task planning while typed tool interfaces constrain actions and a persistent memory component stores user-approved preferences. The controller explicitly separates clarification, retrieval, execution, and response generation, reducing hallucinated actions and unsupported claims. We evaluate multi-turn task completion, tool-call accuracy, memory consistency, recovery after recognition errors, and unsafe-request handling across scheduling, information seeking, and device-control scenarios. The architecture improves successful completion over unconstrained prompting, especially in long dialogues, but clarification behavior and ambiguous user references remain challenging.

aspects.name: Real-time conversational inference
aspects.description: Papers on making language-model voice assistants responsive and interruptible during live conversation. They examine streaming generation, speculative or cascaded processing, latency budgets, barge-in handling, and the trade-offs between response quality and interaction speed.
aspects.bm25_query: voice assistant real-time streaming inference latency streaming ASR incremental generation text-to-speech TTS barge-in endpointing conversational turn-taking
aspects.hyde_abstract: For voice assistants, response timing is a central determinant of conversational quality: a correct answer delivered too late can feel like a failed interaction. We study a real-time language-model voice assistant with streaming speech recognition, incremental decoding, early response planning, and chunked speech synthesis. The system predicts whether an utterance is complete, begins generation before final transcription when confidence is high, and cancels output when the user interrupts. We measure time to first audio, end-to-end response latency, interruption recovery, transcription revisions, task success, and perceived naturalness. Streaming reduces latency substantially and improves user ratings, but premature generation can amplify recognition errors. Adaptive confidence thresholds provide the best quality-latency trade-off across short commands and open-ended requests.

aspects.name: Evaluating voice assistants
aspects.description: Papers that determine how to evaluate voice assistants built on language models, combining speech recognition, conversational quality, task success, latency, factuality, safety and user experience. They address evaluation protocols for interactive, multi-turn spoken settings.
aspects.bm25_query: voice assistant evaluation language model spoken dialogue benchmark task success latency turn-taking speech recognition hallucination safety user satisfaction interactive
aspects.hyde_abstract: Existing language-model evaluations rarely capture the combined challenges of speech recognition, conversational timing, tool execution, and safe behavior in voice assistants. We propose an interactive evaluation framework that measures transcription robustness, response latency, task completion, factuality, dialogue coherence, interruption handling, privacy, and user satisfaction. Evaluators interact with assistants through natural speech rather than isolated text prompts, including disfluencies, corrections, ambiguous references, and background noise. Across several voice-assistant architectures, text-only scores correlate weakly with successful spoken task completion, while latency and recovery from misunderstandings strongly predict human judgments. We recommend reporting component-level and end-to-end metrics separately, with scenario-based safety tests and human assessments of naturalness, control, and trust.

question: How can hospitals safely use LLMs to draft discharge summaries?

aspects.name: Safe discharge drafting
aspects.description: Papers on using large language models (LLMs) to draft hospital discharge summaries while preserving clinical accuracy, completeness, and appropriate medical decision-making boundaries. This includes workflows that keep clinicians responsible for reviewing and authorizing the generated summary.
aspects.bm25_query: LLM large language model discharge summary clinical note hospital clinical documentation drafting safety clinician review human oversight
aspects.hyde_abstract: Large language models may reduce the time required to prepare hospital discharge summaries, but unverified generations can omit diagnoses, medications, follow-up plans, or unresolved problems. We study a clinician-in-the-loop workflow in which an LLM drafts a summary from the electronic health record and a responsible clinician verifies, edits, and signs the final document. The system is evaluated retrospectively and prospectively using factuality, completeness, medication and follow-up agreement, hallucination rate, editing time, and clinician workload. Structured prompting, source-linked evidence, and explicit uncertainty statements reduce unsupported claims compared with unconstrained generation. Clinicians retain final authorship and reject drafts when source information is conflicting or incomplete.
