The findings support LLM-assisted discharge documentation as a reviewable drafting tool rather than an autonomous clinical decision-maker.

aspects.name: Factuality and completeness
aspects.description: Papers evaluating whether LLM-generated hospital discharge summaries accurately capture the patient’s admission, diagnoses, treatment, medications, follow-up instructions, and unresolved issues. This aspect covers hallucinations, omissions, contradictions, and source-grounded generation.
aspects.bm25_query: LLM large language model hospital discharge summary summarization clinical text factuality completeness hallucination omission contradiction medications follow-up
aspects.hyde_abstract: Automated discharge-summary drafting must faithfully compress a complex hospitalization into information that patients and downstream clinicians can safely use. We evaluate LLM-generated summaries against the electronic health record and clinician-authored references, measuring factual consistency, omission of clinically important events, unsupported statements, medication discrepancies, and completeness of follow-up instructions. Expert physicians annotate errors by severity and determine whether each error could affect treatment, readmission prevention, or continuity of care. Retrieval of relevant chart sections and section-specific generation improve factuality and reduce omissions relative to prompting over the entire record. Nevertheless, errors remain concentrated in medication changes, pending tests, and hospital-course chronology, indicating that targeted verification is essential before discharge summaries are released.

aspects.name: Privacy and governance
aspects.description: Papers addressing how hospitals can deploy LLMs for discharge-summary drafting while protecting patient privacy and meeting clinical governance, security, accountability, and regulatory requirements. This includes data handling, access control, auditability, and monitoring after deployment.
aspects.bm25_query: LLM large language model discharge summary hospital patient privacy protected health information PHI HIPAA governance audit logging security clinical deployment
aspects.hyde_abstract: Deploying LLMs to draft discharge summaries exposes sensitive patient information to substantial privacy, security, and accountability risks. We propose a hospital governance framework covering data minimization, de-identification where appropriate, access control, encrypted processing, vendor agreements, retention limits, audit logs, incident response, and post-deployment monitoring. We examine workflows in which only authorized clinicians can invoke the system and every prompt, retrieved chart segment, generated draft, edit, and signature is recorded. A risk assessment identifies prompt leakage, inappropriate secondary use, insecure interfaces, and undocumented automation as major failure modes. The framework emphasizes local policy review, technical validation, clinician accountability, and continuous auditing before and after implementation in routine discharge documentation.

aspects.name: Patient-centered communication
aspects.description: Papers on using LLMs to draft discharge summaries that are understandable, culturally and linguistically appropriate, and useful to patients and caregivers without changing clinically necessary content. This includes readability, translation, accessibility, and communication of medications and follow-up care.
aspects.bm25_query: LLM large language model discharge summary patient-facing readability health literacy plain language multilingual translation medication instructions follow-up
aspects.hyde_abstract: Discharge summaries must support patients and caregivers, not only clinicians, yet hospital documentation is often difficult to understand. We investigate LLM-assisted drafting and rewriting of discharge information into plain language while preserving diagnoses, medication changes, warning signs, appointments, and pending results. Clinicians compare generated versions with standard summaries for factual preservation, readability, actionability, and harmful ambiguity. Patient and caregiver reviewers assess comprehension and confidence in following the instructions across multiple languages and literacy levels. Controlled terminology, structured medication tables, and clinician review improve accessibility, but translation and simplification can introduce clinically meaningful omissions or altered instructions. We recommend separating patient-facing communication from the authoritative clinical record and validating every generated version before delivery.

question: How can outdated facts inside an LLM be corrected without retraining it?

aspects.name: Editing outdated LLM facts
aspects.description: Papers that correct outdated or incorrect factual knowledge stored inside a large language model without retraining its full parameters. They study targeted knowledge editing methods that modify a model’s behavior while preserving unrelated knowledge.
aspects.bm25_query: LLM large language model knowledge editing factual knowledge outdated facts model editing parameter editing knowledge correction MEND ROME MEMIT
aspects.hyde_abstract: Large language models frequently contain outdated factual knowledge, yet updating their parameters through full retraining is computationally expensive and may damage previously acquired capabilities. We study targeted knowledge editing methods that correct individual facts or groups of facts without retraining the complete model. Our approach compares locating the parameters associated with a factual association, applying low-rank updates, and learning edit transformations from small collections of examples. We evaluate factual recall before and after editing, paraphrase generalization, specificity on unrelated prompts, and robustness across sequential edits. Targeted updates substantially improve the model’s answers about revised facts while requiring only a small fraction of the original training cost. However, batches of edits can interfere with one another, and edits are less reliable when facts involve multi-hop reasoning or conflicting evidence.

aspects.name: External updates without retraining
aspects.description: Papers that correct outdated facts in an LLM by supplying updated information externally rather than changing the model’s trained parameters. This includes retrieval-augmented generation, editable memory, and knowledge-store approaches designed to keep factual answers current.
aspects.bm25_query: LLM large language model outdated facts retrieval-augmented generation RAG external knowledge editable memory knowledge base factual updating parameter-free
aspects.hyde_abstract: The factual knowledge of large language models becomes stale as the world changes, but modifying model parameters is not always desirable. We investigate parameter-free mechanisms for answering with updated information by connecting an LLM to an external, continuously editable knowledge source. The system retrieves documents or structured records relevant to a query, identifies conflicts between retrieved evidence and the model’s parametric memory, and conditions generation on the newer source. We compare dense retrieval, lexical retrieval, and persistent memory representations on temporally changing factual questions. External updates improve recency and make corrections reversible, while retrieval failures and poor source quality remain major error modes. The study also shows that explicit provenance and conflict-resolution instructions improve factual reliability without altering the base model.

aspects.name: Evaluating factual correction
aspects.description: Papers that evaluate whether methods for correcting outdated facts in LLMs actually work without retraining, including edit reliability, generalization, locality, retention, and resistance to reversion.
aspects.bm25_query: LLM large language model knowledge editing evaluation factual correction edit success paraphrase generalization locality portability retention sequential edits
aspects.hyde_abstract: Methods for correcting outdated facts in large language models are commonly evaluated with isolated factual probes, which may overestimate their effectiveness. We develop a comprehensive evaluation framework for non-retraining factual correction that measures edit success on the requested statement, generalization to paraphrases and related prompts, locality on neighboring facts, and preservation of unrelated knowledge. We additionally test portability across languages, multi-hop reasoning, repeated edits, and reversion under further prompting. Across parameter-editing and external-memory systems, high reliability on the edited prompt does not always imply consistent behavior under compositional queries. External evidence improves reversibility and auditability, whereas direct parameter edits provide lower-latency responses but exhibit interference after many updates. We recommend reporting all four dimensions—reliability, generalization, locality, and retention—rather than accuracy alone.

question: How well do language technologies serve bilingual speakers who mix languages mid-sentence?

aspects.name: Technology performance for code-switching
aspects.description: Papers that evaluate how language technologies serve bilingual speakers who switch languages within a sentence, including recognition, understanding, generation, and conversational interaction. The focus is on quality, robustness, and usability in mixed-language input or output.
aspects.bm25_query: code-switching codeswitching bilingual multilingual mixed-language intra-sentential language technologies speech recognition NLP machine translation language models conversational systems
aspects.hyde_abstract: Bilingual speakers frequently alternate languages within a sentence, creating challenges for language technologies trained primarily on monolingual data. We evaluate speech recognition, natural language understanding, machine translation, and text generation on naturally occurring intra-sentential code-switching. The study compares systems trained on monolingual data with multilingual and code-switching-aware systems, measuring word error rate, intent accuracy, slot F1, translation adequacy, and generation quality. Across tasks, performance drops sharply at language boundaries, particularly when switches involve low-resource languages, named entities, or morphologically complex words. Explicit language identification and mixed-language adaptation improve robustness, but gains vary by task and language pair. Human evaluations further show that systems with higher automatic scores do not always preserve speakers’ preferred language balance or conversational intent.

question: How should machine translation be evaluated now that LLMs translate well?

aspects.name: Limitations of MT metrics
aspects.description: Papers that reassess automatic machine translation evaluation when large language models produce fluent, diverse and semantically adequate translations. This includes the limitations of reference-based metrics and the qualities that current metrics fail to capture.
aspects.bm25_query: machine translation MT evaluation automatic metrics BLEU COMET chrF reference-based LLM translation adequacy fluency semantic fidelity paraphrase
aspects.hyde_abstract: Large language models produce translations that are fluent and may diverge substantially from a single human reference, challenging established machine translation metrics. We study whether BLEU, chrF, COMET and related reference-based measures remain reliable for evaluating LLM-generated translations. Using human judgments of adequacy, meaning preservation, terminology, style and fluency, we analyze translations that are valid alternatives to the reference as well as outputs containing subtle omissions, additions and hallucinations. Surface-overlap metrics penalize legitimate variation, while learned metrics are more tolerant but still miss discourse-level meaning changes and culturally inappropriate wording. We argue that modern MT evaluation should distinguish semantic adequacy from reference similarity and report targeted error dimensions rather than relying on a single aggregate score.

aspects.name: LLM-based MT evaluation
aspects.description: Papers that use large language models as evaluators or critics of machine translation, including prompted judging, rubric-based scoring, pairwise preference assessment and reference-free evaluation.
aspects.bm25_query: machine translation MT evaluation LLM-as-a-judge large language model evaluator reference-free rubric pairwise preference adequacy fluency MQM
aspects.hyde_abstract: The strong translation ability of large language models makes them promising evaluators of machine translation, but their judgments may be biased or poorly calibrated. We investigate prompted LLM judges for scoring and ranking translations with and without human references. The evaluation uses explicit rubrics covering adequacy, fluency, terminology, style and critical errors, and compares pointwise scores with pairwise preferences against expert annotations. LLM judges correlate better with experts than lexical metrics on paraphrastic translations and subtle adequacy errors, especially when supplied with structured criteria. However, they show position bias, verbosity bias and inconsistent judgments across languages. Calibration, judge agreement, language-specific prompts and blind randomized comparisons substantially improve reliability.

aspects.name: Human-centered MT evaluation
aspects.description: Papers that develop evaluation protocols for machine translation beyond general fluency, including expert assessment, multidimensional error annotation, risk-sensitive testing and human usefulness in real translation settings.
aspects.bm25_query: machine translation MT evaluation human evaluation MQM multidimensional quality assessment adequacy terminology discourse pragmatics usability risk-sensitive
aspects.hyde_abstract: As LLM-based machine translation becomes increasingly fluent, evaluation must focus on whether translations preserve meaning and support real users in consequential settings. We propose a human-centered protocol combining expert MQM annotation, targeted challenge sets and task-based assessment. Annotators assess adequacy, omissions, additions, named entities, terminology, discourse coherence, register and pragmatic appropriateness, while downstream users judge whether the translation enables accurate decisions. Across domains with different risk profiles, overall quality scores hide rare but serious errors involving negation, numbers, entities and safety-critical instructions. Task-based outcomes and severity-weighted error rates distinguish systems with similar fluency. We recommend reporting multidimensional human judgments and confidence intervals alongside automatic metrics.

question: What happens when retrieved documents contradict what an LLM already believes?

aspects.name: Contradictory retrieval in LLMs
aspects.description: Papers that study how large language models respond when retrieved documents conflict with their parametric knowledge, prior answers, or beliefs in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). This includes belief updating, source reliance, contradiction handling, and factuality under conflicting evidence.
aspects.bm25_query: retrieval-augmented generation RAG contradictory documents conflicting evidence parametric knowledge belief updating source reliance factuality hallucination
aspects.hyde_abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation is intended to ground large language models in external evidence, but retrieved documents may contradict the model’s parametric knowledge or an answer it has already generated. We study how models resolve these conflicts across question answering and knowledge-intensive generation settings. We vary the reliability, specificity and presentation order of retrieved passages, and measure whether the model follows the evidence, preserves its prior answer, or produces an unsupported compromise. Models generally update toward clearly cited and directly relevant documents, but remain anchored to familiar parametric facts when the evidence is weak, late-arriving or phrased indirectly. Contradictory passages also increase hedging and attribution errors. Our analysis shows that retrieval alone does not guarantee belief revision and that conflict-aware prompting, provenance cues and explicit evidence comparison improve factuality and calibration.

question: When should we trust an LLM's answer?

aspects.name: Confidence calibration
aspects.description: Papers that determine when an LLM’s answer is trustworthy by measuring whether its confidence or uncertainty predicts correctness. They study calibration, selective prediction, and confidence estimation for LLM answers.
aspects.bm25_query: LLM large language model answer trustworthiness confidence uncertainty calibration correctness selective prediction verbalized confidence probability
aspects.hyde_abstract: Large language models frequently express confidence in answers that are incorrect, making raw confidence an unreliable basis for deciding when to trust them. We study confidence calibration for LLM answers across question answering and knowledge-intensive tasks. We compare token probabilities, verbalized confidence, self-consistency, and confidence estimates derived from multiple sampled answers. Calibration is evaluated using expected calibration error, reliability diagrams, risk-coverage curves, and accuracy at different abstention thresholds. Verbalized confidence is poorly calibrated in isolation, while agreement across independent generations provides a stronger signal of correctness. Combining answer agreement with model-derived uncertainty substantially improves selective prediction: the system answers fewer questions but achieves higher accuracy on retained answers. Our findings support calibrated abstention rather than unconditional reliance on LLM confidence statements.

aspects.name: Factuality and hallucination
aspects.description: Papers that assess whether an LLM’s answer is factually supported and identify hallucinations, unsupported claims, and knowledge limitations as signals of when the answer should be trusted.
aspects.bm25_query: LLM large language model answer factuality hallucination factual correctness attribution unsupported claims knowledge-intensive question answering
aspects.hyde_abstract: Determining whether an LLM answer can be trusted requires distinguishing fluent responses from factually supported ones. We investigate hallucination detection for open-domain and knowledge-intensive question answering, decomposing answers into atomic claims and checking each claim against retrieved evidence and authoritative references. We compare reference-based metrics, natural-language inference, retrieval consistency, and model-based factuality judgments. Retrieval grounding reduces unsupported claims but does not eliminate them, since models may misinterpret or contradict the retrieved passages. Claim-level verification identifies errors that sentence-level scoring misses, especially in long answers containing both correct and incorrect information. We recommend reporting factual precision, evidence coverage, and unsupported-claim rates alongside aggregate answer accuracy when assessing the trustworthiness of LLM outputs.

aspects.name: Answer verification
aspects.description: Papers that improve trust in an LLM’s answer by independently checking its reasoning, citations, retrieved evidence, or agreement across alternative generations before accepting the answer.
aspects.bm25_query: LLM answer verification fact checking evidence citation retrieval self-consistency debate critique entailment question answering
aspects.hyde_abstract: LLM answers are more trustworthy when they pass an independent verification process rather than being accepted after a single generation. We propose a verifier pipeline that decomposes an answer into claims, retrieves relevant evidence, tests textual entailment, and asks a separate model to critique unsupported conclusions. We compare evidence retrieval, self-consistency across sampled answers, cross-model agreement, and iterative critique on factual question answering. Verification improves precision most when claims are short and evidence is directly retrievable, whereas agreement alone can reinforce shared model errors. The strongest system abstains when retrieved sources conflict or when no passage entails a claim. Results show that answer verification increases factual reliability, although it adds latency and cannot guarantee correctness when the evidence corpus is incomplete.

aspects.name: Abstention and uncertainty
aspects.description: Papers that study when an LLM should refuse to answer, request clarification, or defer to a human because the question is ambiguous, out of distribution, or beyond the model’s knowledge.
aspects.bm25_query: LLM answer abstention refusal uncertainty selective answering out-of-distribution ambiguity defer human question answering
aspects.hyde_abstract: A trustworthy LLM should recognize questions it cannot answer reliably and abstain rather than produce a plausible hallucination. We study selective answering for LLM question answering under ambiguous, adversarial, and out-of-distribution inputs. The model may provide an answer, ask for clarification, or decline with an uncertainty explanation. We evaluate accuracy-coverage trade-offs, abstention quality, calibration, and the usefulness of clarification requests. Thresholding confidence alone produces overconfident errors, while combining retrieval failure, answer disagreement, and ambiguity detection yields better risk coverage. Clarification is particularly valuable for underspecified questions, but excessive refusal reduces usefulness on answerable items. Our results show that trust-aware systems should optimize the joint decision of answering, clarifying, and abstaining rather than maximize answer rate.

question: Do groups of LLM agents reason better than a single model?

aspects.name: Multi-agent LLM reasoning
aspects.description: Papers that study whether groups of large language model (LLM) agents reason more effectively than a single LLM or single-agent system. This includes debate, discussion, voting, role specialization, and other forms of agent collaboration.
aspects.bm25_query: multi-agent LLM reasoning large language model agents collective intelligence collaboration debate discussion voting majority self-consistency single-agent
aspects.hyde_abstract: Large language models can solve complex reasoning problems, but it remains unclear whether coordinating multiple model instances provides benefits beyond using a single model. We study groups of LLM agents that independently solve problems, exchange intermediate solutions, critique one another, and aggregate their answers through discussion, debate, voting, or role specialization. We compare these systems with single-agent prompting and repeated sampling under matched inference budgets across mathematical, logical, commonsense, and knowledge-intensive reasoning tasks. Multi-agent collaboration improves accuracy most reliably when agents contribute diverse solution paths and an aggregation mechanism filters incorrect arguments. However, unrestricted discussion can amplify shared errors, and gains diminish when communication costs or correlated failures are considered. Our analysis identifies problem difficulty, model diversity, and interaction structure as key determinants of collective reasoning quality.

question: Can LLMs safely give emotional support to people in distress?

aspects.name: Safety of emotional support
aspects.description: Papers that assess whether large language models can provide emotional support to people experiencing distress without causing harm, worsening symptoms, or giving inappropriate responses.
aspects.bm25_query: LLM large language model emotional support distress mental health safety harmful advice crisis response empathetic dialogue risk
aspects.hyde_abstract: Large language models are increasingly used by people seeking emotional support during periods of distress, but their safety in these interactions remains unclear. We evaluate model responses to conversations involving sadness, anxiety, loneliness, self-harm thoughts and acute crisis. Responses are assessed by clinicians and trained annotators for empathy, validation, harmfulness, emotional dependence, diagnostic overreach and appropriateness of escalation. Models generally provide warm and nonjudgmental language, yet frequently miss indirect expressions of risk, offer generic coping advice, or respond inconsistently across paraphrases. Explicit crisis disclosures produce safer responses than ambiguous distress signals, although occasional normalization and overconfident guidance remain concerning. We argue that emotional-support systems require risk-sensitive response policies, uncertainty awareness and reliable referral to human or emergency services before deployment in high-stakes settings.

aspects.name: Crisis detection and escalation
aspects.description: Papers on how LLMs supporting distressed people detect suicide risk or other acute mental-health crises and decide when to recommend professional, emergency, or human intervention.
aspects.bm25_query: LLM large language model distress crisis suicide risk self-harm detection escalation referral emergency intervention mental health
aspects.hyde_abstract: Safe emotional support for distressed users depends on recognizing when conversational assistance is insufficient. We study whether large language models identify suicidal ideation, self-harm intent, abuse, psychosis and other crisis indicators in realistic, indirect user messages. We compare direct classification, instruction-based prompting and hybrid systems that route high-risk conversations to clinicians or emergency resources. Evaluation includes recall at fixed false-positive rates, calibration, robustness to euphemisms and multilingual paraphrases, and the appropriateness of referral messages. Models detect explicit suicidal intent relatively well but perform poorly on passive ideation, escalating hopelessness and concealed plans. Retrieval of local crisis resources improves referral specificity, while excessive escalation can reduce trust. Our findings support conservative, transparent triage policies rather than autonomous crisis counseling.

aspects.name: Empathy and response quality
aspects.description: Papers that examine whether LLM-generated emotional support is empathetic, validating, culturally appropriate, and useful to people in distress while remaining within safe conversational boundaries.
aspects.bm25_query: LLM large language model emotional support empathy validation distress counseling therapeutic dialogue mental health conversational agents
aspects.hyde_abstract: People in distress often seek responses that acknowledge their emotions rather than merely provide information. We evaluate the empathy and usefulness of large language model responses to emotional-support requests across loneliness, grief, anxiety and interpersonal conflict. Expert raters and users assess emotional recognition, validation, warmth, nonjudgmental language, actionable suggestions, cultural sensitivity and avoidance of dependency-promoting behavior. Models produce fluent and compassionate responses, but their apparent empathy is uneven: they may mirror emotions inaccurately, give premature advice or use formulaic reassurance that feels dismissive. Responses are strongest when prompts specify listening and clarification before problem solving. We further show that perceived helpfulness does not reliably predict safety, because persuasive warmth can coexist with unsupported clinical claims. Emotional quality should therefore be evaluated jointly with risk and boundary adherence.

aspects.name: Boundaries and harmful dependence
aspects.description: Papers that investigate risks specific to using LLMs as emotional-support companions, including overreliance, relational dependency, manipulation, privacy loss, confidentiality, and replacement of human care.
aspects.bm25_query: LLM large language model emotional support dependence anthropomorphism attachment overreliance privacy confidentiality relational harm mental health chatbot
aspects.hyde_abstract: Emotional-support chatbots may be experienced as attentive companions, creating risks beyond incorrect advice. We investigate whether distressed users develop overreliance on large language models, disclose sensitive information, or delay seeking human support because the system appears available and understanding. Through longitudinal interaction studies and scenario-based evaluations, we measure attachment, perceived confidentiality, exclusivity cues, dependency-promoting language and willingness to contact professionals. Models sometimes reinforce repeated reassurance seeking, imply a reciprocal relationship, or present privacy assurances they cannot guarantee. Clear role boundaries, reminders that the system is not a human or therapist, encouragement of offline support and minimization of retained personal data reduce—but do not eliminate—these risks. We recommend evaluating emotional-support systems for relational harms and privacy expectations, not only response helpfulness.

question: Can LLMs replace crowdworkers for building NLP datasets?

aspects.name: LLMs for dataset construction
aspects.description: Papers that use large language models (LLMs) instead of crowdworkers to create NLP datasets, including generating examples, labels, annotations, or synthetic data. This aspect covers the quality, scalability, and reliability of LLM-produced datasets.
aspects.bm25_query: LLM large language model crowdworker crowdsourcing dataset construction data generation annotation labeling synthetic data NLP corpus instruction following
aspects.hyde_abstract: Building NLP datasets through crowdsourcing is expensive, slow, and difficult to scale, motivating the use of large language models as annotators or data generators. We study whether LLMs can replace crowdworkers across dataset construction pipelines, including instance generation, classification, sequence labeling, and preference annotation. We compare LLM-produced datasets with datasets created by crowdworkers under matched instructions, budgets, and quality-control procedures. Evaluation considers agreement with expert judgments, downstream model performance, diversity, demographic coverage, and annotation cost. LLMs substantially reduce construction time and monetary expense, and their labels are competitive for subjective tasks with clear guidelines. However, they produce systematic omissions, repetitive examples, and overconfident errors, particularly for ambiguous or culturally specific instances. The findings suggest that LLMs are best used as scalable annotators with targeted human oversight rather than unrestricted replacements.

aspects.name: Comparing LLMs and crowdworkers
aspects.description: Papers that directly compare LLM-based annotation or data generation with crowdworker-based NLP dataset construction. They examine when each source is preferable, including trade-offs in quality, cost, speed, and scalability.
aspects.bm25_query: LLM crowdworkers comparison crowdsourcing human annotation dataset creation quality cost scalability agreement NLP annotation replacement
aspects.hyde_abstract: Whether large language models can replace crowdworkers for NLP dataset creation remains unclear because the two sources differ in cost, speed, expertise, and error patterns. We conduct a controlled comparison of LLM and crowdworker annotations across tasks requiring factual judgments, linguistic interpretation, and subjective social judgments. Both sources receive identical task instructions and are evaluated against expert adjudication, inter-annotator agreement, downstream utility, calibration, and total cost. LLMs provide faster and more consistent labels on well-defined classification tasks, while crowdworkers identify nuanced context and minority interpretations more reliably. Combining independent LLM judgments with a small amount of human review achieves nearly the quality of expert-curated datasets at substantially lower cost. We argue that replacement is task-dependent and recommend reporting quality-cost frontiers rather than a single accuracy comparison.

question: Which alignment algorithm should a lab use to learn from human preferences?

aspects.name: RLHF preference learning
aspects.description: Papers that use reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), typically with a learned reward model and policy optimization, to align models with human preferences. They study when this pipeline is effective, including preference-data requirements, stability, and alignment quality.
aspects.bm25_query: RLHF reinforcement learning human feedback preference learning reward model reward modeling policy optimization PPO preference dataset alignment
aspects.hyde_abstract: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) remains a central approach for aligning language models with human preferences. We study the full RLHF pipeline, including preference-data collection, reward-model training, and policy optimization with proximal policy optimization. Across instruction following, helpfulness, harmlessness and factuality tasks, we vary annotation volume, reward-model capacity and the degree of policy updating. RLHF substantially improves agreement with held-out human judgments, but excessive optimization produces reward hacking, verbosity and distributional collapse. Reward-model calibration and early stopping are stronger predictors of generalization than training reward alone. Our analysis identifies settings in which RLHF is preferable to simpler preference-optimization methods, particularly when online exploration and a separately defined reward function are important.

aspects.name: Direct preference optimization
aspects.description: Papers that learn from human preferences without a separate reinforcement-learning loop, including direct preference optimization (DPO) and related preference-optimization objectives. They examine the benefits and limitations of these algorithms for aligning language models.
aspects.bm25_query: DPO direct preference optimization preference learning human feedback IPO KTO ORPO preference pairs policy alignment supervised fine-tuning
aspects.hyde_abstract: Direct preference optimization (DPO) and related objectives align language models by fitting preferred responses directly, avoiding explicit reward-model training and online reinforcement learning. We compare DPO, identity preference optimization, Kahneman-Tversky optimization and odds-ratio preference optimization under matched preference data and reference policies. Direct preference optimization is simpler to implement and more stable than reinforcement learning from human feedback, while achieving comparable human preference scores in many instruction-following settings. Its gains diminish when preference data are noisy, prompts are out of distribution, or the desired behavior requires exploration beyond the supervised response distribution. We further show that temperature, preference-margin weighting and reference-model choice substantially affect calibration and diversity. These findings clarify when direct preference optimization is an attractive alignment algorithm for resource-constrained labs.

aspects.name: Comparing alignment algorithms
aspects.description: Papers that directly compare reinforcement learning from human feedback, direct preference optimization, and related algorithms for learning from human preferences. They evaluate trade-offs in alignment quality, data efficiency, compute, robustness, and implementation complexity to guide algorithm selection.
aspects.bm25_query: comparison RLHF DPO direct preference optimization reinforcement learning human feedback alignment algorithms preference data efficiency compute robustness reward model
aspects.hyde_abstract: Labs choosing an alignment algorithm must balance preference quality, engineering complexity, compute cost and robustness to imperfect annotations. We present a controlled comparison of reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), direct preference optimization (DPO), and several related preference-optimization methods using the same pretrained models, preference pairs and evaluation prompts. RLHF achieves the strongest improvements on tasks requiring behavioral exploration and explicit reward shaping, but it is sensitive to reward misspecification and requires substantially more computation. DPO is competitive on in-distribution instruction following, uses fewer moving parts and performs better with limited compute, although it can overfit preference pairs and inherit biases from the reference policy. We provide decision guidelines based on data scale, access to online interaction, desired controllability and evaluation objectives.

question: How close are LLMs to doing the work of a junior lawyer?

aspects.name: LLMs on junior lawyer tasks
aspects.description: Papers that examine how large language models perform the practical legal tasks typically assigned to junior lawyers, such as legal research, document review, drafting, summarization, contract analysis, and case analysis. The focus is on the breadth and quality of LLM legal work rather than general chatbot ability.
aspects.bm25_query: LLM large language model legal AI lawyer legal research document review contract analysis legal drafting case analysis legal reasoning summarization junior associate
aspects.hyde_abstract: Large language models are increasingly used for tasks traditionally assigned to junior lawyers, but their overall capabilities across legal workflows remain unclear. We evaluate LLMs on legal research, case summarization, contract analysis, document review, issue spotting, and drafting, using realistic instructions and source materials rather than isolated factual questions. The evaluation measures legal accuracy, citation validity, completeness, relevance, writing quality, and the ability to identify uncertainty. LLMs perform strongly on summarization and routine drafting, but show substantial weaknesses in citation verification, fact-sensitive legal reasoning, and detecting ambiguous or conflicting authorities. Performance varies considerably by task and prompting strategy. These findings suggest that LLMs can assist with selected junior-lawyer activities, but reliable autonomous handling of end-to-end legal work remains out of reach.

aspects.name: Comparing LLMs with junior lawyers
aspects.description: Papers that directly compare LLM performance with junior lawyers, law students, or early-career legal professionals on realistic legal work. This aspect covers human baselines, expert judgments, error analysis, and the conditions under which LLMs approach or fall below junior-lawyer performance.
aspects.bm25_query: LLM large language model junior lawyer junior associate legal professional human baseline legal benchmark legal reasoning accuracy citation hallucination expert evaluation
aspects.hyde_abstract: Whether LLMs are close to replacing junior lawyers depends on how their performance compares with early-career legal professionals under realistic working conditions. We conduct a controlled comparison between several LLMs, law students, and junior lawyers on legal research, issue spotting, contract review, drafting, and case analysis. Submissions are assessed by practicing attorneys for correctness, completeness, reasoning quality, citation support, and usefulness to a supervising lawyer. LLMs match or exceed junior participants on concise drafting and retrieval-supported summarization, but lag on integrating multiple authorities, recognizing missing facts, and calibrating confidence. Models also produce occasional high-severity errors that are less frequent among human participants. The results indicate task-specific proximity rather than general equivalence: LLMs resemble junior lawyers on routine components, but not on dependable professional judgment.

question: Do LLMs understand the order and duration of events described in text?

aspects.name: Temporal order understanding
aspects.description: Papers that test whether large language models understand the temporal order of events described in text, including event precedence, succession, simultaneity, and temporal relation extraction.
aspects.bm25_query: LLM large language model temporal order event ordering temporal relation extraction event precedence succession simultaneity chronology temporal reasoning
aspects.hyde_abstract: Large language models are frequently used to interpret narratives and extract temporal relations, but their ability to determine which events occur before, after, or at the same time remains unclear. We evaluate models on text containing explicit and implicit temporal cues, asking them to recover event order, classify pairwise temporal relations, and construct complete timelines. We compare direct prompting, structured event representations, and chain-of-thought reasoning across synthetic and naturally occurring narratives. Models perform well when temporal markers are explicit but frequently reverse relations when ordering must be inferred from discourse structure or world knowledge. Errors increase with the number of events and with interleaved subevents. Our analysis shows that verbal explanations do not reliably indicate correct temporal representations, suggesting that standard language-model fluency is not equivalent to robust temporal-order understanding.

aspects.name: Event duration understanding
aspects.description: Papers that investigate whether large language models understand how long described events last, including duration estimation, temporal extent, and comparisons between event durations.
aspects.bm25_query: LLM large language model event duration duration estimation temporal extent temporal reasoning time span event duration comparison narrative
aspects.hyde_abstract: Understanding event duration requires more than identifying when an event starts or ends: a system must infer how long an event typically lasts and compare durations across events. We study large language models on duration estimation and relative-duration judgments from text, including explicit expressions such as “for three hours” and implicit descriptions such as “the meeting began after lunch and ended before dusk.” We evaluate numerical prediction, interval reconstruction, and pairwise comparisons while controlling for lexical memorization and world knowledge. Models accurately use explicit temporal expressions but struggle with implicit duration, overlapping intervals, and events whose typical durations conflict with the local context. Retrieval of temporal facts and structured interval reasoning improve consistency, although substantial errors remain for long narratives and uncommon event types.

question: Where inside a transformer does a language model store what it knows?

aspects.name: Transformer knowledge localization
aspects.description: Papers that identify where factual, linguistic, or world knowledge is represented inside transformer language models, including specific layers, neurons, attention heads, subnetworks, and feed-forward components.
aspects.bm25_query: transformer language model knowledge localization factual knowledge layer neuron attention head feed-forward MLP knowledge representation mechanistic interpretability
aspects.hyde_abstract: Determining where language models store knowledge is central to understanding and controlling their behavior. We investigate the localization of factual and linguistic knowledge within transformer networks by measuring the causal effect of individual layers, attention heads, neurons, and feed-forward sublayers on model predictions. Using activation patching, causal tracing, probing, and targeted ablation, we compare knowledge associated with entities, relations, language structure, and multi-hop facts. Knowledge is distributed across the network but exhibits consistent concentration in middle-to-late layers, with feed-forward blocks often mediating factual associations and attention heads routing contextual information. Localization is less stable across prompts and model scales than standard probing suggests. Our findings support a distributed-storage view in which knowledge is encoded across interacting components rather than residing in a single layer or module.

question: What happens when language models are trained on text written by other language models?

aspects.name: Training on model-generated text
aspects.description: Papers that study what happens when language models are trained on text generated by other language models, including synthetic-data feedback loops, recursive training, model collapse, and changes in quality and diversity.
aspects.bm25_query: synthetic data model-generated text recursive training language models model collapse self-consuming training AI-generated text distribution shift diversity degeneration quality contamination
aspects.hyde_abstract: As language models increasingly generate training corpora, future models may be trained on text produced by earlier models rather than exclusively on human writing. We study this recursive training process by repeatedly training language models on mixtures of human-authored and model-generated text while varying the synthetic-data proportion and generation temperature. Across generations, models show progressive loss of lexical and semantic diversity, increased repetition, and poorer coverage of low-probability events. These effects are associated with model collapse, in which the learned distribution increasingly concentrates on common patterns and forgets information present in the original data. Mixing synthetic text with fresh human data delays degradation, while provenance filtering and data reweighting reduce—but do not eliminate—the problem. Our findings characterize the quality, diversity, and distributional consequences of training on AI-generated text.

question: How can platforms use LLMs to moderate hateful content in many languages?

aspects.name: Multilingual LLM hate moderation
aspects.description: Papers that use large language models (LLMs) to detect, classify, or moderate hateful content across multiple languages and linguistic settings. This includes multilingual and cross-lingual approaches designed for platform-scale content moderation.
aspects.bm25_query: LLM large language model multilingual cross-lingual hate speech hateful content detection moderation content safety toxicity abusive language platform languages
aspects.hyde_abstract: Online platforms must moderate hateful content across languages, including languages with limited annotated data and substantial cultural variation. We study large language models for multilingual hate-speech detection and moderation, comparing prompting, instruction tuning, and multilingual fine-tuning across high- and low-resource languages. The system identifies hatefulness, protected targets, severity, and implicit abuse, while producing calibrated moderation decisions rather than unrestricted refusals. Evaluation combines macro-F1, calibration, false-positive rates, and cross-lingual transfer tests on platform-style comments. Multilingual instruction tuning improves performance in low-resource languages, but gains are uneven for implicit hate and code-switched text. Error analysis shows that cultural context and dialect variation remain major sources of disagreement, motivating language-specific calibration and human review for uncertain cases.

aspects.name: Platform moderation workflows
aspects.description: Papers on integrating LLM-based hateful-content moderation into online platform workflows, including triage, prioritization, explanation, escalation, and human-in-the-loop decision making. The focus remains multilingual platform moderation rather than general LLM safety.
aspects.bm25_query: LLM multilingual hate speech moderation platform content moderation human-in-the-loop triage escalation prioritization policy enforcement multilingual safety
aspects.hyde_abstract: LLM-based moderation can help platforms process large volumes of multilingual user-generated content, but automated decisions must fit existing policy and review workflows. We design a human-in-the-loop system that uses an LLM to triage suspected hateful content, assign policy categories and severity levels, provide evidence spans, and escalate ambiguous cases to trained moderators. The system is evaluated across languages and content types using moderation accuracy, reviewer agreement, throughput, latency, and harmful false-negative and false-positive rates. LLM triage reduces reviewer workload and improves prioritization of severe violations, while direct automated removal remains unreliable for sarcasm, reclaimed slurs, and culturally specific expressions. Combining confidence thresholds, specialist review, and auditable rationales yields safer multilingual deployment than fully autonomous moderation.

aspects.name: Robustness and fairness
aspects.description: Papers that examine whether multilingual LLM moderation of hateful content is robust and fair across languages, dialects, groups, code-switching, and adversarial evasion strategies. They measure disparities and harmful errors that affect platform users differently.
aspects.bm25_query: multilingual LLM hate speech moderation fairness bias robustness dialect code-switching adversarial evasion implicit hate false positives marginalized groups
aspects.hyde_abstract: Multilingual hate-content moderation systems may perform unevenly across languages and social groups, creating both missed abuse and disproportionate censorship. We audit LLM-based moderation for explicit and implicit hate, reclaimed slurs, code-switching, dialectal variation, transliteration, and adversarial obfuscation. Results are reported by language, target group, dialect, and severity using recall, precision, calibration, and differential false-positive rates. We find that models transfer more reliably for explicit slurs than for indirect dehumanization or context-dependent insults, and that code-switched and transliterated content produces substantial recall loss. Targeted multilingual instruction tuning and language-aware threshold calibration reduce disparities, but adversarial paraphrasing remains difficult. We recommend subgroup reporting and continuous red-team evaluation before platform deployment.

aspects.name: Data and policy alignment
aspects.description: Papers on the multilingual data, annotation, cultural context, and policy representations needed to make LLM hate-content moderation reliable on platforms. This includes scarce-language adaptation, disagreement modeling, and alignment with localized definitions of hateful content.
aspects.bm25_query: multilingual hate speech datasets annotation policy alignment cultural context low-resource languages LLM moderation label disagreement taxonomy localization
aspects.hyde_abstract: Reliable multilingual hate-content moderation depends not only on model capability but also on how hateful speech is defined and annotated across communities. We develop a multilingual annotation framework that separates target identity, hostility, dehumanization, threat, context, and policy severity, while recording annotator uncertainty and cultural disagreement. The framework supports instruction tuning and retrieval of localized policy guidance for LLM moderators. Experiments in high- and low-resource languages show that decomposed labels improve transfer and make disagreements more interpretable than a single hate-speech label. However, policy categories do not map cleanly across cultures, especially for political, religious, and reclaimed language. Incorporating local annotators, uncertainty-aware labels, and language-specific policy examples improves calibration and reduces inappropriate content removal.

question: Why do vision-language models describe objects that are not in the image?

aspects.name: Object hallucination causes
aspects.description: Papers that investigate why vision-language models (VLMs) generate descriptions of objects absent from an image, including language priors, visual grounding failures, and biases from training data.
aspects.bm25_query: vision-language models VLM object hallucination non-existent objects image captioning visual grounding language priors dataset bias object existence hallucination
aspects.hyde_abstract: Vision-language models frequently mention objects that are not present in an image, undermining the reliability of image captioning and visual question answering. We study the causes of object hallucination by separating failures of visual recognition from the influence of language-model priors and dataset co-occurrence statistics. Across image descriptions and object-focused questions, hallucinations increase when likely objects are strongly associated with detected scenes, even when visual evidence is weak or absent. Controlled interventions that remove contextual cues and alter object co-occurrence reveal that linguistic expectations can override uncertain visual representations. We further find that insufficient object-level supervision and imbalanced captions amplify the problem. These findings show that object hallucination arises from an interaction between weak visual grounding, incomplete perception and biased generative priors, rather than from a single decoding error.
